p: The first Hebrew word can open a full sentence or a time clause. Both readings are old.
b: The Hebrew bereshit has no "the," and the word reshit is usually followed by "of" ("the beginning of..."). So Rashi (died 1105) read the verse as a time clause: "When God began to create the heavens and the earth, the earth was shapeless..." The 1985 Jewish Publication Society translation follows him, as does the NRSV ("In the beginning when God created"; NRSVue "When God began to create"). The ancient Greek, Latin and Aramaic versions all read a full sentence, "In the beginning God created," and most translations keep it. The choice matters for one question: does 1:1 describe God making everything from nothing, or does it begin with a dark, watery earth already there (1:2)? Later writings make creation from nothing explicit (2 Maccabees 7:28, in the Catholic and Orthodox canon; compare Hebrews 11:3), though scholars debate whether they, or Genesis 1, teach it in the later technical sense (Gerhard May).

a: In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.
p: The first verse has seven Hebrew words. Sevens run through the whole account.
b: Umberto Cassuto counted the sevens built into 1:1–2:3. The first verse has 7 Hebrew words and the second has 14. "God" comes 35 times, "earth" 21 times, and "it was good" 7 times (the seventh time as "very good"). The last paragraph (2:1–3) has 35 words and three lines that each name "the seventh day." Most scholars accept the counts, though some are debated (it depends on how small words are counted). The point is plain: the whole account is built to lead up to the seventh day. Ancient Near Eastern texts also used seven-day patterns, for example the seven days of the storm in the Babylonian flood story and the seven days of building in a Ugaritic poem.

t: Elohim: a plural word for one God
p: The word for God is plural in form, but its verb is singular. The plural shows greatness, not many gods.
b: Elohim is plural in form (the ending -im) and can mean "gods" when it refers to the gods of the nations (Exodus 20:3). When it means Israel's God, it takes a singular verb, as here: "God created" (bara, "he created"). Hebrew grammarians call this a plural of majesty or fullness. Elohim is the only name for God in 1:1–2:3, and it appears 35 times there. From 2:4 on, the personal name YHWH joins it (see the note on "the LORD God" at 2:4). Many Christian readers since the early church have seen a hint of the Trinity in the plural form; most scholars, Jewish and Christian, think the grammar alone cannot carry that weight.

t: Bara: a verb only God does
p: In the Hebrew Bible only God is ever the subject of this verb.
b: Bara, "create," never has a human subject in the Hebrew Bible, and it never names any material that God works with. It comes three times at the key points of this chapter: the heavens and earth (1:1), the first living creatures (1:21), and humans (1:27, three times in one verse). The word alone does not prove creation from nothing, since God also "creates" a pure heart (Psalm 51:10) and a new Jerusalem (Isaiah 65:18). John Walton argues that it is mainly about giving things their role and order; most commentators think it includes bringing things into being. The idea that God made everything from nothing became explicit in later Jewish and Christian teaching (2 Maccabees 7:28; Romans 4:17; Hebrews 11:3).

a: The earth was shapeless and empty.
t: Something before verse 2? The gap theory
p: Some read a long gap between 1:1 and 1:2. Most Hebrew scholars do not think the grammar allows it.
b: The "gap" or "ruin and restoration" theory says 1:1 describes an original creation, which was ruined, perhaps when Satan fell, and 1:2 should read "the earth became shapeless and empty"; the six days then describe a re-creation. Thomas Chalmers proposed it in 1814 to make room for the ages of geology, and the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) made it popular among American evangelicals. Most scholars, including most young-earth and old-earth writers today, reject it. The verb hayetah normally means "was," not "became," and the sentence pattern (a noun first, then the verb) describes the situation at the start, not a new event. The view is now held by few, though it survives in some Pentecostal and dispensational teaching.

p: A rhyming pair for a place where nothing can live: a waste and a void.
b: Tohu va-vohu is a sound-pair, like "helter-skelter." Tohu elsewhere means a trackless desert (Deuteronomy 32:10; Job 6:18) or something empty and useless (Isaiah 41:29). The pair comes again only in Jeremiah 4:23, where Jeremiah sees the land after judgment "shapeless and empty," with no light, as if creation had been undone. The rest of the chapter answers the two words: days 1–3 give the world shape by dividing it; days 4–6 fill it. Isaiah 45:18 says God did not create the earth to be tohu but formed it to be lived in.

p: The Hebrew word sounds like Tiamat, the sea monster of the Babylonian creation story. Is there a link?
b: Tehom, "the deep," is the primeval ocean. In the Babylonian Enuma Elish (written in its known form by about 1100 BC), the god Marduk kills the sea goddess Tiamat and splits her body in two to make sky and earth. Hermann Gunkel (1895) argued that Genesis borrowed and demythologized that story. Today most scholars agree there is a link in ideas but not in words: tehom and Tiamat come from a common Semitic root for "sea," and tehom has no article and no personality here (David Tsumura). Genesis has no battle. The deep simply lies there until God speaks. Other poems in the Bible do picture God defeating the sea monster (Psalm 74:13–14; Isaiah 51:9).

p: Ruach can mean spirit, wind or breath. The verb pictures a bird hovering over its young.
b: Ruach elohim can be "the Spirit of God," "a wind from God," or even "a mighty wind" (the word "God" sometimes works like "very"). Some Jewish translations (JPS 1985) and the NRSV read "wind." Most Christian and many Jewish readers read "Spirit," as elsewhere in the Bible (Exodus 31:3; Psalm 104:30). The verb merachefet occurs again only in Deuteronomy 32:11, of an eagle hovering over its nest. A wind also blows over the waters after the flood (8:1), when the world is made again. Christians have long seen the Holy Spirit here, at work with the Father and the Word (Psalm 33:6; John 1:1–3).

p: God makes the world by speaking. Psalms, John and Hebrews build on this.
b: "God said" comes ten times in the chapter. The rabbis noticed: "By ten sayings the world was created" (Mishnah Avot 5:1). In Babylonian and Egyptian stories the gods fight, mate or shape things by hand. Here God speaks and it happens. Psalm 33 sums it up: "The heavens were made by the LORD's word" (Psalm 33:6), and "he said it, and it was" (Psalm 33:9). John 1:1–3 takes up the theme: "In the beginning was the Word... Through him everything came to exist." Hebrews 11:3 says "the ages were set in order by a word from God." Some Egyptian texts do have the god Ptah create by thought and speech (the Memphite Theology), a real but distant parallel.
r: Psalm 33:6–9; Psalm 148:5; John 1:1–3; Hebrews 11:3; 2 Corinthians 4:6; 2 Peter 3:5

a: God saw the light, that it was good
p: The refrain comes seven times. "Good" means fit for its purpose and pleasing, not only morally right.
b: Hebrew tov is a broad word: pleasant, useful, beautiful, right. God sees that each work does what it was made for. The refrain appears seven times, the last as "very good" (1:31). It is missing on the second day (unless one follows the Septuagint, see the variant at 1:8), and it is said twice on the third. The first thing in the Bible that is "not good" is the man alone (2:18). The verdict matters for how Jews and Christians have viewed the physical world: matter, the body, food and sex are not evil in themselves (1 Timothy 4:4).

a: Evening came, and morning came: day one.
p: The central debate of Genesis 1. Readers have held at least five views. See the chapter page for each one.
b: Ordinary days (young-earth creationists, the majority of Jewish and Christian tradition): yom with a number and with "evening and morning" means a normal day, and Exodus 20:11 grounds the work week in it. Long ages (day-age: Hugh Ross; William Jennings Bryan at the Scopes trial): yom can mean a time period (2:4), a day is like a thousand years to God (Psalm 90:4), and the seventh day has no end. God's work-days (analogical: C. John Collins): the days are real but are God's days, told by analogy to a worker's week. A literary frame (Arie Noordtzij, Meredith Kline, Henri Blocher; Augustine had already read the days as non-chronological): the week is a framework that arranges creation by topic, not time. Temple inauguration (John Walton): seven real days in which God assigns the world its functions, not its material origins.

p: The Hebrew says "day one" with no article. The later days are "a second day," "a third day."
b: Hebrew uses the number "one" (echad) here, not the word for "first" (rishon), and leaves off "the" for days one to five. Only the sixth and seventh days have "the." Rashi said the Torah says "one" because God was still alone: the angels had not yet been made. Others note that Hebrew can use "one" for "first" in counting (8:13 "the first of the month" is literally "one of the month"). The missing article may show that the days are not yet a series, or simply that Hebrew style varies. Young-earth writers stress that a day with a number always means an ordinary day elsewhere; others reply that Genesis 1 is a unique text.

p: Raqia is something hammered out flat. Ancient readers pictured the sky as a solid vault.
b: The verb raqa means to stamp or beat out, as metal is hammered into thin plates (Exodus 39:3; Numbers 16:39). The Greek translators chose stereoma, "something firm," and the Latin firmamentum, from which the KJV's "firmament" comes. Job 37:18 asks if one can "spread out the skies, hard as a cast metal mirror." Many scholars (Paul Seely, John Walton) hold that the writer shared the ancient picture of a solid sky holding back waters above, and that God spoke to Israel within that picture. Others (many young-earth and old-earth writers) take raqia as the open sky or the atmosphere, described as it looks to us. Translations differ: "expanse," "vault," "dome," "sky."
r: Exodus 39:3; Job 37:18; Psalm 19:1; Psalm 104:2; Isaiah 40:22; Ezekiel 1:22

p: Israel's poets also speak of waters above the heavens. What were they?
b: Psalm 148:4 calls on "the waters above the heavens" to praise God, and the flood begins when "the windows of the sky" open (7:11). In the ancient Near East the blue sky was widely thought to be a barrier holding back an ocean above it. Some readers take the waters above as clouds and rain (compare Job 26:8). In 1961 John Whitcomb and Henry Morris popularized a "vapor canopy" (an idea Isaac Vail had put forward in 1874) of water around the early earth that fell as the flood rain and had earlier sheltered long human lives; many young-earth writers have since dropped the idea for physical reasons. Readers who see ancient cosmology here say the point is theological: God set limits to the waters, which no longer threaten.

p: The Hebrew word does not match a modern category. The text does not address evolution directly.
b: Min, "kind," is a general word for a sort or group (Leviticus 11:14–19 lists birds "by their kind"). It is not the same as the modern biologist's "species." Young-earth creationists hold that God created separate original kinds, each of which could vary within limits (the field some call baraminology, from Hebrew bara and min), and many place a "kind" near the level of a biological family. Old-earth creationists also often read fixed kinds. Evolutionary creationists (such as the BioLogos organization) say the phrase describes the order of nature that people can see, plants and animals reproducing true to type, not a claim about how kinds came to be. The phrase comes ten times in the chapter.

p: The word for "appointed times" is Israel's word for its festivals. The lights keep the calendar of worship.
b: Moadim, "appointed times," is the word Leviticus 23 uses for the LORD's festivals: Passover, Weeks, Tabernacles. So the sun and moon are given a job in worship: they mark the days, months and feast seasons. The "signs" are probably signals of time and weather (Jeremiah 10:2 warns Israel not to be terrified by "signs in the sky" as the nations are). Nothing here supports astrology. Psalm 104:19 echoes the verse: "He made the moon to keep the appointed times." The Dead Sea community and the book of Jubilees later argued fiercely about whether the calendar should follow the sun or the moon, building partly on this verse.

a: God made the two big lights
p: The text avoids the words "sun" and "moon," which were also names of gods. Many read a quiet protest.
b: Hebrew shemesh, "sun," sounds like Shamash, the Babylonian sun god, and the moon was worshiped as Sin at Ur and Haran (11:31). Genesis 1 calls them only "lights" or "lamps" (me'orot, the word used for the lampstand in the tabernacle, Exodus 25:6), gives them a job, and mentions the stars almost as an afterthought. Many scholars read this as a deliberate polemic against star worship (Gerhard Hasel; compare Deuteronomy 4:19). The order also raises a question readers have asked since Origen: how were there days and light (1:3–5) before the sun? Young-earth writers answer that God provided a light source at first; day-age writers (Hugh Ross) that the sun was made in 1:1 and became visible from the earth on day four; others say the account is arranged by topic, not timeline (see the chapter page).

t: The sea monsters are only animals
p: Tanninim are dragons of the sea in Israel's poems. Here God simply creates them.
b: This is the second time the chapter uses "created." Tanninim can be large sea animals (Psalm 148:7), snakes (Exodus 7:9, Aaron's staff), or the sea dragon that God crushes in poetry (Psalm 74:13; Isaiah 27:1, where it stands beside Leviathan). In Canaanite poems from Ugarit (about 1300 BC), Baal and the goddess Anat defeat Yamm (Sea), the dragon (tnn) and Litan, the coiling serpent. Genesis takes the most feared creatures of the ancient imagination and lists them among God's creatures, with no fight at all. Psalm 104:26 even pictures Leviathan playing in the sea God made.

p: God speaks in the plural. Readers have offered at least four explanations.
b: The Trinity: from the Epistle of Barnabas (5:5) and Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 62) on, many Christians have read the plural as the Father speaking with the Son and the Spirit. The heavenly court: God consults the angels, his council (1 Kings 22:19–22; Job 1:6; Isaiah 6:8). Rashi held this, saying God set an example of humility by consulting those below him, and many modern scholars agree. Plural of majesty, like a king's "we"; critics answer that Hebrew has no clear example of this with verbs. Self-encouragement, "Come, let's..." (Cassuto). The same plural returns at 3:22 and 11:7. Justin and Barnabas wrote in the second century; Philo, a Jewish thinker of the first, already said God spoke here to his helpers.

p: The Hebrew adam here means the human race, not yet the man named Adam.
b: Adam is a collective noun, "humankind," and the next verb is plural: "let them rule." In 1:27 it has "the" (ha-adam, "the human") and takes first a singular, then a plural pronoun: "he created him... he created them." Chapters 2–3 use ha-adam, "the man," for the first person. The word becomes a personal name without "the" (4:25; 5:1–5), and in a few places the Hebrew vowels make it uncertain (2:20; 3:17, 21). The Plain English Translation writes "humankind," "the man" or "Adam" to follow the Hebrew in each place.

a: in our image, as our likeness
p: A tselem is a statue or a figure. Ancient kings were called the image of a god. Here every human is.
b: Tselem means a carved or cast figure, often an idol (2 Kings 11:18) or a model (1 Samuel 6:5); demut means a likeness or pattern. In Egypt the king was called the living image of a god (the name Tutankhamun means "living image of Amun"), and Assyrian letters call the king the image of Bel or Shamash. Genesis gives this royal title to every man and woman and links it at once to ruling the earth. Views of what the image is: the mind and soul (much of classic theology), a relationship with God, a royal task of representing God on earth (Clines, Middleton), or all of these. Jewish and Christian readers agree that the image grounds human dignity (9:6; James 3:9). The New Testament calls Christ the image of God (Colossians 1:15).

a: male and female he created them
p: Jesus quotes this line, with 2:24, in his teaching on marriage.
b: Both male and female are in God's image, in the same breath. Jesus quotes the line, "from the start of creation, 'male and female he made them'" (Mark 10:6; Matthew 19:4), together with 2:24, to show that marriage was meant to last. Paul's "there is no male and female" in Christ (Galatians 3:28) echoes the Greek wording of this verse. Some rabbis read the shift from "him" to "them" as a first human who was both male and female, later divided (Genesis Rabbah 8:1, citing Rabbi Jeremiah ben Elazar); Philo read two creations, one ideal and one physical. Most readers take "him" as the human race and "them" as its two sexes.

p: Strong verbs, used of kings and conquest. Readers argue whether they mean stewardship or license.
b: Kavash, "subdue," is used for conquering a land (Numbers 32:22; Joshua 18:1) and even forcing people into slavery (Jeremiah 34:11). Radah, "rule," is a king's word (Psalm 72:8; 1 Kings 4:24). In 1967 the historian Lynn White Jr. blamed this verse for Western exploitation of nature. Most interpreters answer that the rule belongs to a king who is God's image and must rule like God, with care: the man is set in the garden "to work it and to guard it" (2:15), and the Law protects land and animals (Leviticus 25:2–7; Deuteronomy 22:6–7). Psalm 8 celebrates the same royal role with wonder, not pride.

p: Humans and animals are given plants to eat. Meat is first allowed after the flood (9:3).
b: The plain sense is that people and animals were vegetarian at first; God permits meat only in 9:3. Young-earth creationists draw a wider conclusion: there was no animal death, predation or disease until human sin, so the fossil record, full of death, must come after the fall and mostly from the flood (Romans 5:12; 8:20–22). Old-earth and evolutionary creationists reply that the verses describe what God provided, not a ban on all death; that Romans 5 speaks of human death; and that Psalm 104:21 praises God for feeding the lions their prey. The prophets look forward to a peaceful creation where "the lion, like the ox, will eat straw" (Isaiah 11:6–9; 65:25).

p: The final verdict is stronger, and the sixth day is the first with "the."
b: After making humans, God looks at "everything," not just one work, and calls it tov me'od, "very good." The Hebrew also adds "look" (hinneh), as if seeing through God's eyes. This is also the first day with the article: "the sixth day." Rashi saw a hint of the sixth day of the month Sivan, when Israel later received the Torah, as if creation hung on that condition. Genesis Rabbah 9:7 finds even the "evil inclination" in "very good": without desire no one would build a house, marry or have children. Christians cite the verse against teachings that the physical world is evil.

p: The verb shavat means to stop or cease. It gives the Sabbath its name.
b: Shavat means first to stop doing something (Joshua 5:12, the manna "stopped"). God does not rest because he is tired (Isaiah 40:28); he rests because the work is done. From this verb comes Shabbat, the Sabbath, though the word "Sabbath" itself never appears in Genesis. The Ten Commandments ground the weekly rest in this verse (Exodus 20:11), and Exodus 31:17 adds a bold word: on the seventh day God "stopped and caught his breath" (vayyinafash). Deuteronomy 5:15 gives a second reason, the rescue from slavery in Egypt.

a: God blessed the seventh day and set it apart as holy
p: The seventh day has no "evening and morning." Readers draw very different conclusions.
b: Days one to six close with "evening came, and morning came"; the seventh does not. Augustine saw in this an endless rest that God offers his people (Confessions 13.36). Hebrews 4:3–10 says God's works "had been done ever since the world was founded," so his rest has been open since then, and it still waits to be entered. Day-age readers argue that if the seventh day is still going on, the other days can be long too. Young-earth writers answer that Exodus 20:11 compares God's seventh day to Israel's ordinary one. John Walton reads the seventh day as the climax of a temple dedication: in the ancient world a god "rests" when he takes his throne in his finished temple (compare Psalm 132:7–8, 13–14). This is the first thing in the Bible God calls holy: a time, not a place.

p: This formula, "this is the family history of," opens ten sections of Genesis.
b: Toledot comes from the verb "to father" (yalad) and means "what was fathered": descendants, or the story of what came from someone. The formula "these are the toledot of X" divides Genesis into ten sections: the heavens and earth (2:4), Adam (5:1), Noah (6:9), Noah's sons (10:1), Shem (11:10), Terah (11:27), Ishmael (25:12), Isaac (25:19), Esau (36:1, 9) and Jacob (37:2). Each section usually tells what came from the person named: "the family history of Terah" is mostly the story of Abraham. Scholars debate whether 2:4a closes the first account (a summary at the end, like a label on a clay tablet) or opens the second; evangelical commentators mostly read it as a heading, as everywhere else in Genesis, while many critical scholars read it as the close of the first account.

a: On the day the LORD God made earth and heaven,
p: Chapter 2 tells creation again, in a different order and style. Is it a second source or a close-up?
b: In 1:1–2:3 God (Elohim) speaks and orders a cosmos over six days, ending with humankind. In 2:4–25 the LORD God shapes a man from soil before plants and animals appear in the story, then animals, then the woman. Classic source theory assigns 1:1–2:4a to P (usually dated to the 500s BC, though some date it earlier) and 2:4b–25 to J (traditionally older, though many recent scholars date the non-Priestly text later). They note the change in God's name, vocabulary and order. Traditional readers see one author who first gives the big picture and then zooms in on the sixth day and the garden (Cassuto, Kitchen, Collins); they point out that 2:5 concerns field plants and farming, not all plants, and that 2:19 can be read "had formed." Both sides agree the final book sets the two side by side on purpose.

p: Here God's personal name appears for the first time. Most English Bibles print it "the LORD."
b: The four letters YHWH are God's own name, revealed to Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:14–15). Out of reverence, Jewish readers stopped saying it aloud and read Adonai, "the Lord," instead; the Septuagint wrote Kyrios, "Lord." This site follows most English Bibles and prints "the LORD" in small capitals; "Lord" in ordinary letters stands for Adonai. The scholarly guess at its pronunciation is "Yahweh." The double name "the LORD God" (YHWH Elohim) appears 20 times in chapters 2–3 and only once more in the Torah (Exodus 9:30). The rabbis said the two names show two sides of God: Elohim his justice, YHWH his mercy (Genesis Rabbah 12:15).

p: The rare word 'ed may mean a mist (KJV), a spring, or the underground waters.
b: 'Ed appears only here and in Job 36:27. The Greek has "a spring" and Targum Onkelos "a cloud"; the KJV has "a mist." Many scholars connect it with Akkadian edû, the flood or swell of underground water, which fits a land watered from below, as Mesopotamia and Egypt were watered by rivers, not by rain. Some young-earth writers have built on 2:5–6 to argue that it never rained before the flood; most commentators say the verse only describes the moment before the garden was planted.

p: Was Adam one historical man, the first of all humans, or a figure for humanity? Christians hold several views.
b: Traditional (most Jews and Christians through history, young-earth and many old-earth creationists): God made Adam directly from the soil a few thousand years ago, the father of all people (Acts 17:26; Romans 5:12–19). Catholic teaching (Pius XII, Humani generis, 1950) allows that the body may have developed from earlier life, holds that each soul is created directly by God, and insists on one first parent of all humans. An historical pair within a larger population (C. John Collins; some evolutionary creationists): God chose or specially formed a real couple as humanity's head. An archetype (John Walton): Adam and Eve were real but the story presents them as representatives of all people, and says nothing about biological origins. A figure (Peter Enns; most critical scholars): Adam is Everyman, as his name "Human" suggests. Since the 2000s, genome studies suggesting a large ancestral population (Venema and McKnight, 2017) have sharpened the debate.
r: Romans 5:12–19; 1 Corinthians 15:21–22; 1 Corinthians 15:45; Acts 17:26; Luke 3:38; 1 Timothy 2:13

p: The man (adam) comes from the ground (adamah). English "human" and "humus" make a similar pair.
b: The play on words ties people to the soil they are made from, work (2:5, 15) and return to (3:19). The verb yatsar, "shape," is a potter's word (Jeremiah 18:2–6; Isaiah 64:8), and the same verb is used for the animals (2:19). Here only the man has God's breath (neshamah) breathed into him, a close, personal act (compare 7:22). In the Babylonian Atrahasis epic the gods make humans from clay mixed with the blood of a slain god, so that people can do the gods' hard labor. Genesis also uses clay, but the human is made to tend God's garden, not to be a slave.
orig: הָאָדָם עָפָר מִן־הָאֲדָמָה (ha-adam afar min ha-adamah)

t: Not "a soul" in the later sense
p: The KJV says "a living soul." The Hebrew nefesh chayyah is used of animals too.
b: Nefesh chayyah means a living creature, a breathing being. The same phrase describes fish, birds and land animals (1:20, 24; 2:19), where translations rightly write "creature." So the verse does not say that God put a soul into a body. It says that a body of dust, given God's breath, became a living person. The idea of an immortal soul distinct from the body developed later, under Greek influence and through later Jewish and Christian reflection. Paul quotes this verse from the Greek, "the first man Adam became a living soul," and contrasts Christ, "a life-giving spirit" (1 Corinthians 15:45).

p: Eden sounds like the Hebrew for "delight." The Greek word for the garden gave us "paradise."
b: In Hebrew eden means "delight" or "luxury" (Psalm 36:8). Many scholars also compare a Sumerian and Akkadian word edin, "plain" or "steppe." Eden is the region; the garden lies in its east. The Septuagint translated "garden" with paradeisos, a Persian loanword for a walled royal park. That word came into English as "paradise," used for the restored world and for heaven (Luke 23:43; 2 Corinthians 12:4; Revelation 2:7). Ezekiel calls Eden "the garden of God" on "the holy mountain of God" (Ezekiel 28:13–14).
r: Ezekiel 28:13–14; Ezekiel 31:8–9; Isaiah 51:3; Joel 2:3; Luke 23:43; Revelation 2:7

p: Eating from it would let a person live forever (3:22). It returns in the Bible's last chapter.
b: The tree of life is never forbidden; only the second tree is. After the fall, the way to it is guarded (3:24). Proverbs uses the image for wisdom and a gentle tongue (Proverbs 3:18; 15:4). Revelation pictures it again beside the river of the New Jerusalem, open to all (Revelation 2:7; 22:2, 14). Mesopotamian literature knows a similar hope: in the Epic of Gilgamesh the hero finds a plant called "Old Man Grows Young," and a snake steals it while he bathes (Tablet XI). Both stories link a snake with the loss of endless life, though the plots and meanings differ.

a: the tree of knowing good and evil
p: The tree's name is a puzzle. Readers suggest moral autonomy, mature wisdom, all knowledge, or sexual awareness.
b: Deciding for oneself what is good and evil, taking God's place as judge (many Jewish and Christian readers; compare Isaiah 5:20). Mature or royal wisdom: children "do not yet know good from bad" (Deuteronomy 1:39), in Hebrew the same tov va-ra as the tree's name, and a wise king can "discern good and evil" (2 Samuel 14:17; 1 Kings 3:9). Some argue the knowledge was not bad in itself but was to be received from God in time. Everything: "good and evil" as a pair meaning all things. Sexual awareness: some critical readers point to the nakedness that follows (3:7), but the man and woman are already told to be fruitful (1:28). In 3:22 God says the humans have become "like one of us" in this knowing.

a: A river goes out from Eden
p: Two of the four rivers are known. The other two have never been identified for certain.
b: The Tigris (Hebrew Hiddeqel, Akkadian Idiglat) and Euphrates flow through Mesopotamia, modern Iraq. Pishon and Gihon are unknown. Havilah is linked with Arabia (10:7, 29; 25:18), and Cush is usually Nubia, south of Egypt (10:6), though some think of the Kassites of Mesopotamia. Suggestions for Eden's site include the head of the Persian Gulf, where several rivers once met (Juris Zarins), and Armenia, where the Tigris and Euphrates rise. Young-earth writers usually say the flood reshaped the world, and later rivers took the old names. Others read the geography as a picture: one river from God's presence watering the four corners of the world (compare Ezekiel 47:1–12).

p: The second river shares its name with the spring beside the temple city.
b: Gihon is also the name of the spring in Jerusalem's Kidron Valley, where Solomon was crowned (1 Kings 1:33, 38) and from which Hezekiah cut his tunnel (2 Chronicles 32:30). The prophets and psalms picture a river flowing from God's temple to give life (Psalm 46:4; Ezekiel 47:1–12; Joel 3:18; Zechariah 14:8), and Revelation 22:1–2 joins that river with the tree of life. Many scholars, including Gordon Wenham and G. K. Beale, see the shared name as one sign that the writer pictures Eden as the first sanctuary, the place where God lives with people.
r: 1 Kings 1:33; 2 Chronicles 32:30; Psalm 46:4; Ezekiel 47:1–12; Zechariah 14:8; Revelation 22:1–2

a: to work it and to guard it
p: The same two verbs describe the priests' duties at the tabernacle. Many readers see Eden as a temple.
b: Avad, "work" or "serve," and shamar, "guard" or "keep," appear together for the Levites who serve and guard the tabernacle (Numbers 3:7–8; 18:5–7). Gordon Wenham listed other links: God "walking about" in the garden (3:8; Leviticus 26:12), an entrance on the east guarded by cherubim (3:24; Exodus 26:31), gold and onyx (2:12; Exodus 25:7; 28:9–12), and a tree like the lampstand. So the first man is pictured as a priest in God's sanctuary as well as a farmer. Literary-theological readers (Walton, Beale) build much on this; others think the links are suggestive but not proof. The Targum understood "work" as studying Torah and "guard" as keeping its commandments.

t: Why did they not die that day?
p: God warns of death "on the day" they eat. They live on for years. Readers explain this in several ways.
b: The Hebrew doubles the verb for emphasis, as in 2:16. "On the day" can mean simply "when" (2:4; 1 Kings 2:37, 42), so the sentence was passed that day though carried out later. Spiritual death: the bond with God died at once (Ephesians 2:1). Mortality: from that day they were bound to die, cut off from the tree of life (3:22–24). A day of the LORD: Jubilees 4:30 and Justin Martyr noted that Adam died at 930, within one "day" of a thousand years (Psalm 90:4). The snake's flat denial, "You will not die" (3:4), turns on this verse.

a: a helper who is his match
p: The Hebrew word ezer is used most often for God helping his people.
b: Ezer means help or rescue, and in the Hebrew Bible it most often names God: "my help comes from the LORD" (Psalm 121:1–2; also Exodus 18:4; Psalm 33:20). So the word itself says nothing about lower rank. Kenegdo, "like opposite him" or "corresponding to him," means a partner who matches him face to face, as none of the animals can (2:20). The KJV's "help meet" ("a help fit for him") was later run together as "helpmate." How this partnership relates to leadership in marriage is debated among Christians (compare 1 Corinthians 11:8–9; Ephesians 5:21–33).

p: Without vowels the Hebrew could be "for the man" or "for Adam." The Masoretic vowels read "Adam."
b: The consonants l'dm can be read la-adam, "for the man," or le-adam, "for Adam." The Masoretic scribes chose "Adam" here and in 3:17 and 3:21, while elsewhere in chapters 2–3 the word has the article, "the man." Many translations (NRSV, JPS) put "the man" in all these places; others (KJV, BSB) put "Adam." The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic vowels. It is clearly a personal name from 4:25 on.

p: Tsela usually means "side," as in the side of a building. The rabbis argued over which it was.
b: Elsewhere tsela is the side of the ark of the covenant or of the tabernacle, or a side room in the temple (Exodus 25:12; 26:20; 1 Kings 6:5), never a body part. The verb in 2:22 is a builder's word too: God "built" the woman. Some rabbis read "one of his sides": the first human was made with two faces, and God split it (Genesis Rabbah 8:1). Others read "rib." Either way, the woman is made of the same stuff as the man. Samuel Noah Kramer suggested a link with a Sumerian myth where a goddess Nin-ti, whose name can mean both "lady of the rib" and "lady who makes live," heals Enki's rib. The pun works only in Sumerian, and most scholars now think the connection is weak.

a: This one will be called Woman,
p: The first human words are a poem with a pun: "woman" (ishshah) from "man" (ish).
b: The Hebrew ish ("man, husband") and ishshah ("woman, wife") sound alike, much like English "man" and "woman," though scholars think the two words come from different roots. "Bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh" is a formula for kinship and loyalty: the tribes say it to David (2 Samuel 5:1), and Laban to Jacob (29:14). Walter Brueggemann argued that it is covenant language, a promise of loyalty in weakness and strength. "This one" (zot) is said three times in the Hebrew, as if the man cannot stop pointing.

p: Jesus and Paul both quote this verse, in the Greek form "the two will become one flesh."
b: Jesus joins this verse to 1:27 to teach that marriage is God's doing: "What God has joined together, let no one separate" (Matthew 19:4–6; Mark 10:6–9). Paul uses it to warn against sex with a prostitute (1 Corinthians 6:16) and as a picture of Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31–32). In a world where a bride usually moved to her husband's family, it is striking that the man is the one who "leaves." "Cling" (davaq) is a covenant word, used of Israel holding fast to the LORD (Deuteronomy 10:20) and of Ruth clinging to Naomi (Ruth 1:14). The verse is the narrator's comment, applying the story to every marriage.
r: Matthew 19:4–6; Mark 10:6–9; 1 Corinthians 6:16; Ephesians 5:31–32; Deuteronomy 10:20; Malachi 2:15

p: "Naked" (arummim) is one letter from "shrewd" (arum) in the next verse.
b: Hebrew arummim, "naked," and arum, "shrewd" or "cunning" (3:1), are a pun that links the two scenes. The humans are open and unashamed; the snake is crafty. After they eat, they will know they are "naked" (eirummim, 3:7, 10–11) and will be ashamed and afraid. Shame in the Bible is often about being exposed before others (Isaiah 47:3). Clothing returns as a sign of God's care when he dresses them (3:21).

p: The text calls it a wild animal God made. Later Jewish and Christian writers saw the devil behind it.
b: Genesis says only that the snake was one of the creatures "the LORD God had made," unusually shrewd, and able to speak; it is judged as an animal (3:14). Later readers saw more. The Wisdom of Solomon (2:24) says "through the devil's envy death entered the world." Revelation names "that ancient serpent, who is called the Devil and Satan" (Revelation 12:9; 20:2), and Paul and Jesus allude to the scene (John 8:44; 2 Corinthians 11:3; Romans 16:20). Some rabbinic texts say the angel Samael rode the snake (Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer 13). Snakes were sacred or feared across the ancient Near East: a snake steals the plant of life from Gilgamesh, and in Egypt the serpent Apophis fights the sun god each night. Critical scholars usually read the story as about a real snake, explaining why people and snakes are enemies.

a: Is it really true that God said
p: The snake calls God only "God," not "the LORD God," and twists the command into a total ban.
b: The Hebrew opens with af ki, "So, indeed...?", a phrase of surprise or sneer. In chapters 2–3 the narrator calls God "the LORD God" every time, but the snake and the woman say only "God" (Elohim), as if speaking of a distant power rather than the LORD who walks in the garden. The snake also turns God's generous "You may eat, yes eat, from every tree" (2:16) into "you must not eat from any tree." The first temptation in the Bible starts with doubt about what God said, and then about whether God is good (3:5).
orig: אַף כִּי־אָמַר אֱלֹהִים (af ki amar Elohim)

p: God never said "do not touch." The rabbis saw here the danger of adding to God's word.
b: In 2:17 God forbade eating from the tree, not touching it. The woman adds a stricter rule. The rabbis taught Israel to "make a fence around the Torah" (Mishnah Avot 1:1), adding cautious rules so as not to break a commandment. But they also used this verse as a warning: one who adds to God's word takes away from it (Genesis Rabbah 19:3). In one story the snake pushed her against the tree, and when she touched it and did not die, he said, "So you will not die from eating either" (Avot de-Rabbi Natan, version A, 1). Deuteronomy 4:2 forbids both adding to and taking from the commandments.

p: Elohim can mean "God" or "gods." The KJV and the Greek have "as gods."
b: The Hebrew ke-lohim may mean "like God" or "like gods" (divine beings), and the plural participle that follows ("knowing") is grammatically plural either way. The Septuagint (hōs theoi), the Vulgate and the KJV took it as "gods"; most modern versions read "like God," since God is the one who knows good and evil (3:22). Either way the offer is to become something more than human by grasping. Christian readers often set this beside Philippians 2:6, where Christ, who was in the form of God, "did not consider equality with God something to be grasped."

a: she took some of its fruit and ate
p: What changed when they ate? Augustine, the rabbis and the Eastern churches answer differently.
b: Genesis never uses the words "sin" or "fall" here; "sin" first appears in 4:7. Augustine (about AD 400) taught that all humans sinned "in Adam" and inherit both guilt and a corrupted nature (original sin), reading Romans 5:12 in its Latin form "in whom all sinned." Protestant theology mostly follows him; Catholic teaching calls original sin a state "contracted, not committed," the loss of original holiness rather than personal guilt (Catechism 404–405). The Eastern Orthodox churches speak of ancestral sin: we inherit death and a weakened nature, not Adam's guilt. Jewish tradition generally holds that each person is born with a good and an evil inclination (the yetzer hara, see 6:5) and chooses freely; Adam brought death but not inherited guilt. Critical scholars often read the story as a tale of growing up and losing innocence. The New Testament contrasts Adam with Christ (Romans 5:12–21; 1 Corinthians 15:22).

p: The fruit is never named. The apple came from a Latin pun.
b: Genesis says only "fruit" (peri). The rabbis guessed a fig (because fig leaves follow in 3:7), grapes, wheat or the citron (Talmud, Berakhot 40a; Genesis Rabbah 15:7). Western art settled on the apple, probably helped by a pun in Latin, where malum means both "apple" and "evil." The "Adam's apple" in the throat comes from the same tradition.

p: The man stood beside her the whole time. The text does not support the idea that he was away.
b: The phrase immah, "with her," and the plural "you" in the snake's speech (3:1–5) suggest the man was present and silent. Some artists and writers (Milton's Paradise Lost, for example) placed Adam elsewhere, and the phrase is missing from the Latin Vulgate, but the Hebrew and Greek have it. God holds the man fully responsible (3:17), and the New Testament usually names Adam as the one through whom sin entered (Romans 5:12–19). 1 Timothy 2:14 says it was the woman who was deceived, a verse much debated today.

a: in the breezy part of the day
p: The Hebrew says "at the wind of the day," usually taken as the evening breeze. A few read a storm.
b: Le-ruach ha-yom is literally "at the wind (or spirit) of the day." Most take it as the time of the cool afternoon breeze (KJV "in the cool of the day"); the Septuagint has "in the afternoon." Jeffrey Niehaus has argued for "in the wind of the storm," reading the scene as a terrifying arrival of God in judgment, like Sinai, but most commentators think that is unlikely here. "Walking about" (mithallekh) is the verb used for God's presence moving in Israel's camp and tabernacle (Leviticus 26:12; Deuteronomy 23:14; 2 Samuel 7:6).

p: God's first question to a human. The rabbis heard in it the lament of exile.
b: God surely knows where the man is; the question invites him to come out and answer. Genesis Rabbah 19:9 notes that the Hebrew letters of ayyekkah ("where are you?") can be read eikhah, "How...!", the first word of Lamentations, and draws the parallel: as God brought Adam into the garden, gave him a command, and sent him out when he broke it, so God brought Israel into the land and sent it into exile. Hasidic teachers later read the question as God asking every person, "Where are you in your life?"

a: On your belly you will crawl
t: Did the snake once have legs?
p: Some old readings say the snake once walked and talked. Others say the curse gives new meaning to how snakes move.
b: Josephus says the snake lost its legs and its speech as punishment (Antiquities 1.50), and Genesis Rabbah 20:5 has angels cut off its feet. Many modern readers think the verse gives a sad meaning to what snakes already did, as the rainbow (9:13) is given a new meaning. "Eating dust" is a picture of humiliation and defeat (Psalm 72:9; Micah 7:17). Isaiah sees it as lasting even in the new creation, when the wolf and lamb feed together: "dust will be the snake's food" (Isaiah 65:25).

p: Christians since the 100s have read this as the first promise of Christ. Some ancient Jewish readers did too.
b: Christian: Irenaeus (about AD 180) read the woman's offspring as Christ, who crushes the snake (Against Heresies 5.21.1); the verse came to be called the protoevangelium, the "first gospel." Paul echoes it: "God will soon crush Satan under your feet" (Romans 16:20; compare Galatians 4:4; Revelation 12). Jewish: most medieval commentators (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Ramban) read the lasting enmity between humans and snakes, and some later readers the evil inclination; the Palestinian Targums (Neofiti and Pseudo-Jonathan) say there will be a remedy for the wound "in the days of King Messiah." Critical scholars (Westermann, von Rad) mostly read a lasting struggle between humans and snakes, and behind it between people and evil. Zera, "offspring," can be one child or many; the Hebrew uses "he" (singular), and the Greek autos keeps a masculine pronoun even though its word for seed is neuter.

a: and you will strike him on the heel
p: The same verb describes both blows. Translations often make one stronger than the other.
b: The Hebrew uses one verb, shuf, for both blows. It is rare (Job 9:17; Psalm 139:11), and its meaning is uncertain: "bruise" (KJV), "crush" or "strike." Many translations write "crush" for the head and "strike" for the heel, which makes the contrast plain but is not in the Hebrew. The Septuagint uses "watch for" both times, perhaps reading a similar verb (sha'af, "lie in wait"). The contrast is in the targets: a blow to the head kills a snake; a bite to the heel wounds, perhaps fatally, but the victor still stands.

p: The word for pain is the same as the man's "painful labor" in the next verse.
b: Itsavon means painful toil or hardship. It is used for the woman (3:16) and the man (3:17), and again in 5:29. "Your pain and your pregnancies" is likely a pair meaning "the pain of your pregnancies." Carol Meyers argued that in Israel's farming villages it meant both a woman's hard field labor and many pregnancies: "your toil and your pregnancies." Either way, the blessing to be fruitful (1:28) now comes with suffering.

a: Your desire will be for your husband,
p: Is the woman's "desire" love or a wish to control? Is the husband's rule God's plan or a result of sin?
b: Teshuqah, "desire," appears only three times: here, in 4:7 (sin's desire for Cain, which he must "rule"), and in Song of Songs 7:10 (the lover's desire for his beloved). The Septuagint has "your turning" (apostrophē), as if reading a related word. Susan Foh (1975) argued from 4:7 that the woman will want to control her husband, and he will dominate her. Others take it as longing for her husband despite the pain of childbirth (Rashi; many modern scholars). Most interpreters, including many complementarians, read "he will rule over you" as describing the damage of sin, not God's ideal; egalitarians add that the gospel aims to undo it (Galatians 3:28).

a: the ground is cursed on your account
p: God curses the snake and the ground, never the man or the woman. The curse echoes through the Bible.
b: God curses only the snake (3:14) and the ground; to the humans he announces consequences. Lamech names Noah hoping for relief from "the ground that the LORD cursed" (5:29), and after the flood God promises never again to curse the ground (8:21). Paul says creation was "subjected to futility" and waits to be set free (Romans 8:20–22), and Revelation ends with "no more curse" (Revelation 22:3). Thorns become a lasting picture of a ruined field (Isaiah 5:6); the soldiers' crown of thorns (Matthew 27:29) has been read by many Christians as an echo.

a: and to dust you will go back.
p: These words are behind "ashes to ashes, dust to dust" and Ash Wednesday.
b: The man was shaped from "dust of the ground" (2:7) and now hears that he will return to it. The theme recurs in Job 34:15, Psalm 90:3, Psalm 103:14, Psalm 104:29 and Ecclesiastes 3:20 and 12:7 ("the dust returns to the earth... and the spirit returns to God"). Christian burial services have long used "earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust," and on Ash Wednesday many churches say "Remember that you are dust, and to dust you shall return." Daniel 12:2 and 1 Corinthians 15:47–49 look beyond the dust to resurrection.
r: 2:7; Psalm 90:3; Psalm 103:14; Ecclesiastes 3:20; Ecclesiastes 12:7; Daniel 12:2; 1 Corinthians 15:47–49

p: Chavvah sounds like the word for "living." The Greek translators simply called her Zoe, "Life."
b: The name Chavvah is explained by chay, "living": she is "the mother of everyone living." The Septuagint translated the name here as Zōē, "Life" (elsewhere it writes Heua). The man names her right after hearing that they will die, a hopeful act. Genesis Rabbah 20:11 notes that in Aramaic chivya means "snake," and plays on that too. Paul names her twice (2 Corinthians 11:3; 1 Timothy 2:13).

p: God himself clothes the guilty pair. Christians saw a first sacrifice; some rabbis saw garments of light.
b: Their fig leaves (3:7) are replaced by something lasting that God provides. Many Christian readers see the first animal death as a covering for sin, pointing ahead to sacrifice (compare Hebrews 9:22), though the text does not say how the skins were obtained. Jewish readers stress God's kindness: God clothes the naked, and so should we (Talmud, Sotah 14a). Genesis Rabbah 20:12 reports that Rabbi Meir's Torah scroll read 'or with an aleph, "light," instead of 'or with an ayin, "skin": "garments of light." Other readers see the human body itself as the "garment of skin" (Origen was accused of teaching this).

t: A sentence God does not finish
p: The Hebrew breaks off in the middle. The expulsion is described as protection as well as punishment.
b: In Hebrew God's sentence begins "and now, so that he does not stretch out his hand..." and never ends; the next verse simply tells what God did. Many translations finish it with a dash; the Plain English Translation makes it a question. Some church fathers saw mercy in this: it would be a disaster for people to live forever in a state of sin, so death and the exile from the tree were also a gift (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.23.6; Gregory of Nazianzus). The plural "one of us" returns from 1:26 (see the note there).

p: Cherubim are winged guardians. Their images later stand in the tabernacle and temple.
b: The cherubim (singular cherub) are not chubby babies but powerful winged beings, perhaps like the Mesopotamian karibu and the huge human-headed winged bulls (lamassu) that guarded Assyrian palace gates. Gold cherubim stood on the ark of the covenant (Exodus 25:18–22), were woven into the curtain that closed off the Most Holy Place (Exodus 26:31), and stood in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:23–29), whose entrance faced east. Ezekiel saw them carrying God's throne (Ezekiel 1; 10). The flaming, turning sword may be lightning, as God's weapon (Psalm 104:4). The way back to the tree of life is shut, and the whole Bible asks how it will be opened again (Hebrews 10:19–20).
r: Exodus 25:18–22; Exodus 26:31; 1 Kings 6:23–29; Ezekiel 10:1–22; Ezekiel 28:14; Hebrews 10:19–20; Revelation 22:14

a: I have gained a man, with the LORD
p: Eve's words make a pun on Cain's name. "With the LORD" is one of the hardest phrases in Genesis.
b: Qaniti, "I have gained" or "I have made," sounds like Qayin, Cain. The verb qanah can mean "create" (14:19, 22; Proverbs 8:22), so Eve may be saying, "I have made a man, together with the LORD," a proud or joyful echo of God's creating. Et YHWH is usually read "with the help of the LORD" (Septuagint "through God"). Martin Luther read et as the object marker, "I have gotten a man: the LORD," thinking Eve believed her son was the promised offspring of 3:15. Few scholars follow him, but the idea shows how early readers linked the two verses. "Man" (ish) for a newborn is unusual and may echo 2:23.

p: Abel's name is the word Ecclesiastes uses for "vapor" or "meaningless."
b: Hevel means a breath or a puff of vapor, something brief that vanishes (Psalm 39:5; 144:4). It is the key word of Ecclesiastes: "Vapor of vapors... everything is vapor" (Ecclesiastes 1:2, often rendered "meaningless" or "vanity"). Abel never speaks, has no children, and dies young, and his name fits. No one in the story explains it; the narrator lets it stand. The New Testament remembers Abel as "righteous" (Matthew 23:35; Hebrews 11:4; 1 John 3:12).

a: as a gift to the LORD
p: Both brothers bring a minchah, a word for a gift or tribute. It is not specifically a blood sacrifice.
b: Minchah is a present given to win or show favor, like Jacob's gift to Esau (32:13) or tribute paid to a king (Judges 3:15). In the later Law it is the grain offering (Leviticus 2). So the word does not by itself mark Cain's offering as wrong because it lacked blood; both brothers bring a minchah, each from his own work. The difference the text points to is in what was brought and how (see the note on 4:4).

a: The LORD looked kindly at Abel and at his gift
p: The text does not say. Readers offer four main answers.
b: The quality of the gift: Abel brings "the firstborn" of his flock "and of their fat," the best (Leviticus 3:16), while Cain brings simply "some of the fruit," not the first fruits (Exodus 23:19). Many Jewish and Christian commentators hold this. The heart of the giver: "By faith Abel offered God a fuller sacrifice than Cain's" (Hebrews 11:4); Cain's deeds were evil (1 John 3:12); God looks on Abel first, then on his gift. Blood: some Christian writers argue that only an animal sacrifice could please God, but minchah (4:3) argues against this. God's free choice: God often favors the younger brother (Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Ephraim, David), and Cain's test is how he responds. How the brothers knew is not said; some ancient readers, followed by Rashi, imagined fire falling from heaven on Abel's gift.
r: Hebrews 11:4; Hebrews 12:24; 1 John 3:12; Jude 11; Exodus 23:19; Leviticus 3:16

a: sin is crouching at the door
p: The first time the Bible uses the word "sin," it is pictured as an animal or demon waiting to pounce.
b: Rovets, "crouching," is used of animals lying down (49:9). E. A. Speiser compared the Akkadian word rabitsu, a demon that lurks at a house door. The grammar is odd: "sin" is feminine but "crouching" is masculine, which supports reading it as a crouching creature. The last line closely echoes 3:16: "its desire is for you, but you must rule over it." The verb timshol could be a command ("you must rule"), a promise ("you will rule") or a permission ("you may rule"). John Steinbeck built East of Eden (1952) on the Hebrew timshel, "thou mayest," as a word of human freedom.

a: Cain turned on Abel his brother and killed him
p: Because the Hebrew leaves Cain's words out, the Targums filled in a debate about justice.
b: The Palestinian Targums (Neofiti and Pseudo-Jonathan) give Cain and Abel a whole argument in the field. Cain says, "There is no judgment and no judge, no world to come, no good reward for the righteous and no punishment for the wicked." Abel answers that there is. Genesis Rabbah 22:7 offers other quarrels: over dividing the world, over where the temple would stand, or over a woman. The word "brother" appears seven times in 4:2–11, pressing home that this is the first murder, of a brother by a brother. 1 John 3:12 makes Cain the model of hatred, and Jesus puts Abel first among the righteous whose blood was shed (Matthew 23:35).

p: Cain uses the verb for guarding the garden (2:15). Abel the shepherd kept flocks; Cain refuses to keep his brother.
b: Shomer, "guard" or "keeper," is the verb of 2:15, where the man is set in the garden "to guard it," and it is God's own title in Psalm 121:4–5 ("he who keeps Israel"). The irony is sharp: Abel was a "keeper" of sheep (ro'eh), and Cain sneers that he is not his brother's keeper. God's question echoes 3:9 ("Where are you?") and asks for a confession that does not come.

a: Your brother's blood has a voice, and it is crying
p: The Hebrew says "bloods." The rabbis read it as Abel and all the children he would have had.
b: Demei is plural, "bloods," which in Hebrew often means bloodshed. The Mishnah, warning witnesses in a capital trial, reads it as "his blood and the blood of his descendants" and draws the famous lesson: "whoever destroys a single life is counted as if he destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves a single life, as if he saved a whole world" (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5). "Crying" (tso'aqim) is the cry of the oppressed that God hears (Exodus 3:7; 22:23). Hebrews 12:24 contrasts it: the blood of Jesus "speaks a better word than the blood of Abel."
orig: קוֹל דְּמֵי אָחִיךָ צֹעֲקִים (qol demei achikha tso'aqim)
r: Exodus 3:7; Exodus 22:23; Job 16:18; Hebrews 12:24; Revelation 6:9–10; Matthew 23:35

p: A rhyming pair: a drifter with no home. The land of Nod (4:16) means "Wandering."
b: Na va-nad joins two verbs for staggering and roaming, like "wandering and wavering." Cain, the farmer, loses the ground that fed him. He then settles in "the land of Nod" (4:16), from nod, "wandering": he lives in the Land of Restlessness. No such place is known on any map. The rabbis also read Cain's words in 4:13 as a question of repentance: "Is my sin too great to be forgiven?" (Genesis Rabbah 22:13; the Hebrew avon can mean both sin and its punishment).

a: anyone who finds me will kill me
p: Cain fears other people, then finds a wife and builds a city. Where did they come from?
b: Adam's other children: Genesis says Adam had "sons and daughters" (5:4), and many readers, from Jubilees (4:1, 9, which names Cain's sister-wife Awan) to young-earth writers today, hold that Cain married a sister or niece, before the Law forbade it (Leviticus 18:9). Other humans: some have argued that people lived outside the garden. Isaac La Peyrère (1655) proposed people before Adam; John Walton and others today suggest Adam and Eve were not the only humans, and the story assumes this. A story told for its meaning: many critical scholars think the Cain story once stood on its own, in a world already full of people. The text does not say.

a: the LORD set a sign for Cain
t: The sign of Cain protected him
p: The "mark" was for Cain's protection, not his shame. Its later use for race was a misuse.
b: Ot, "sign," is the same word used for the rainbow (9:12) and circumcision (17:11). Here it guards Cain's life. The text does not say what it was; the rabbis guessed a horn, a letter of God's name, or a dog that walked with him (Genesis Rabbah 22:12). In America, some white Christians in the 1700s and 1800s claimed the mark was dark skin and used that to defend slavery, and some leaders of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints taught it to explain their ban on Black priests, a teaching that church formally disavowed in 2013. Nothing in the text links the sign to skin or race. Compare the protecting mark in Ezekiel 9:4–6.

a: Cain was then building a city
t: The first city and the first arts
p: Civilization begins in the line of the murderer. Mesopotamian stories credit culture to wise sages.
b: The first city is built by the wanderer who was told he would have no home, perhaps a sign of defiance. His descendants found herding (4:20), music (4:21) and metal-working (4:22). Mesopotamian tradition credited the arts of civilization to seven sages, the apkallu, who lived before the flood, and Babylonian lists name the first city as Eridu. Genesis also gives culture a human origin before the flood, but it does not make the inventors divine, and it shows the arts growing alongside violence (4:23–24). Augustine built The City of God (book 15) on the contrast between Cain's earthly city and the city of God.

a: Tubal-cain, who hammered out every kind of tool from bronze and iron
p: Iron working became common in the Near East only after about 1200 BC.
b: Bronze (copper with tin) came into wide use in the Near East during the 3000s and 2000s BC; smelted iron tools became common only after about 1200 BC, though objects made from meteoric iron and a few smelted pieces are much older. Critical scholars see the mention of iron as a sign that the list reflects later times. Traditional readers note early iron objects and say the text names the founder of a craft, not the date it spread. The name "Cain" also means "smith" in Aramaic and Arabic, and the Kenites (Numbers 24:21–22), perhaps a clan of metalworkers, share the name. Jabal, Jubal and Tubal all sound like the verb yaval, "to bring" or "to lead."

p: Lamech boasts of seventy-sevenfold revenge. Jesus calls for seventy-sevenfold forgiveness.
b: Lamech, seventh from Adam in Cain's line, takes two wives (the first in the Bible) and turns God's protection of Cain (4:15) into a song of revenge. When Peter asks if he should forgive "up to seven times," Jesus answers "seventy-seven times" (Matthew 18:21–22). The Greek there, hebdomēkontakis hepta, is the Septuagint's exact wording in this verse, and many scholars think Jesus deliberately reverses Lamech. (Some translations of Matthew read "seventy times seven.") The "boy" (yeled) Lamech killed may mean a young man, not a child.

p: Seth's name sounds like "set in place." The word "offspring" links him to the promise of 3:15.
b: Shet, Seth, sounds like shat, "he has set" or "appointed." Eve calls him "another offspring" (zera), the word God used in 3:15 for the woman's offspring who would strike the snake. From here the hope runs through Seth's line in chapter 5 to Noah, and later to Abraham's offspring (12:7; 22:17–18). Luke traces Jesus' line back to "the son of Enosh, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God" (Luke 3:38).

a: people began to call on the LORD's name
t: When did people learn the name YHWH?
p: Here worship of the LORD by name begins. Exodus 6:3 seems to say the name was first revealed to Moses.
b: Source critics point to this verse as key evidence: the Yahwist (J) source used the name YHWH from the beginning, while the Elohist and Priestly sources say it was first revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14–15; 6:3). Traditional readers answer that Exodus 6:3 means the patriarchs did not know God fully in the character the name expresses, as the one who keeps his promises. Jewish tradition read the verb huchal, "began," as chullal, "was profaned": people began calling idols by God's name, and idolatry began (Targum Onkelos; Rashi; Genesis Rabbah 23:7). The Septuagint has "this one hoped to call on the name of the Lord God." "Calling on the name" means public worship and prayer (12:8; Joel 2:32; Romans 10:13).

a: This is the book of the family history of Adam
t: Are there gaps in the genealogies?
p: Adding up the ages gives about 1,656 years from Adam to the flood. Are the lists complete?
b: Closed lists: many readers add the numbers to date creation. Archbishop James Ussher (1650) reached 4004 BC, and young-earth creationists today generally place creation about 6,000 to 10,000 years ago. They note that each link gives an exact age at fathering, which seems meant for counting; even if names were skipped, the stated ages leave no room for added years. Open lists: William Henry Green (1890) argued that Hebrew "fathered" can mean "became the ancestor of," that biblical lists often skip names (compare Matthew 1:8 with 1 Chronicles 3:11–12), and that Scripture never totals these years. Most old-earth evangelicals follow him. Stylized lists: critical scholars and many others note that Adam to Noah and Shem to Abram are each ten generations, a shape that suggests design (Mishnah Avot 5:2).

a: Adam lived 130 years and fathered a son
p: Babylonian lists also name long-lived figures before the flood, with reigns of tens of thousands of years.
b: The Sumerian King List (best known from a clay prism of about 1800 BC, the Weld-Blundell Prism) begins: "After kingship came down from heaven, kingship was in Eridu." Eight kings in five cities rule for 241,200 years in all, the first, Alulim, for 28,800 years; "then the flood swept over." The Babylonian priest Berossus (about 290 BC) gives ten kings before the flood ruling 432,000 years, the tenth being the flood hero. Most scholars see a real relationship of form: a list of ten great figures before a flood, then shorter lives after. The differences are large: Genesis lists ordinary fathers, not kings, its numbers are far smaller, and every one of them dies.

a: in his likeness, by his image
p: The words of 1:26 come back reversed. The image of God is passed on through human families.
b: God made humans "in our image, as our likeness" (1:26); Adam fathers Seth "in his likeness, by his image." The echo shows that the image of God did not vanish after the fall: it is handed on to Adam's children, as 9:6 and James 3:9 also assume. Some Christian readers add that Seth also inherits Adam's fallen state. The same words describe a son resembling his father in Mesopotamian texts, and Luke 3:38 calls Adam the "son of God" in a similar sense.

t: Lives of nearly a thousand years
p: Readers take the long lives as literal, as symbolic numbers, or as honoring the ancestors.
b: Literal (traditional Jews and Christians; young-earth creationists today): people lived this long before the flood, and lifespans fell afterward, as chapter 11 shows. Proposed reasons include a better early environment or the slow buildup of genetic damage. Symbolic numbers: Cassuto and others noted that many of the ages are built from multiples of five and of seven, in the Mesopotamian base-60 style, and Enoch's 365 matches the days of a year. Ancestral honor: some scholars read the numbers as a way of giving the ancient fathers weight, as Mesopotamian lists did on a much larger scale. Psalm 90:10 sets the later norm at seventy or eighty years.

t: Two family lines that look alike
p: Several names in Seth's line look like names in Cain's line. One list or two?
b: Compare Cain's line (4:17–18) with Seth's: Cain and Kenan; Enoch and Enoch; Irad and Jared; Mehujael and Mahalalel; Methushael and Methuselah; Lamech and Lamech. Each line also ends with three sons in its last generation (4:20–22; 5:32). Many critical scholars think one old list was handed down in two forms, used by two sources. Traditional readers see a deliberate contrast: the seventh in Cain's line (Lamech) boasts of murder, while the seventh in Seth's line (Enoch) walks with God, and the two Lamechs speak in opposite spirit (4:23–24; 5:29). Both lines, Cain's and Seth's, have been read as the city of man and the city of God.

p: Enoch's life matches the days of a year. Babylon's seventh king before the flood was also taken to the gods.
b: Enoch is seventh from Adam (Jude 14), and his 365 years match the solar year. The seventh king in the Babylonian lists, Enmeduranki of Sippar, the city of the sun god, was said to be taken into the gods' presence and taught the secrets of heaven. James VanderKam and other scholars think these traditions shaped the later Jewish books of Enoch, where Enoch learns the secrets of the calendar (1 Enoch 72–82). Whether Genesis itself knew the Babylonian story is debated. The Genesis account is very brief, with no secret knowledge, only a life of walking with God.

p: Every other entry ends "and he died." Enoch's does not.
b: The verb laqach, "took," is used of Elijah's going up (2 Kings 2:3, 5, 9–10) and of God taking the righteous to himself (Psalm 49:15; 73:24). "Walked with God" (hithallekh et ha-Elohim) is used only of Enoch and Noah (6:9), a close daily friendship. The Septuagint renders "Enoch pleased God, and he was not found, because God moved him," and Hebrews 11:5 quotes it: "By faith Enoch was carried off, so that he did not see death, and 'he was not found, because God had carried him off.'" Some rabbis read "God took him" as a quiet death (Genesis Rabbah 25:1); most Christian and much Jewish tradition read it as a going up alive, which inspired the books of Enoch.

p: By the Hebrew numbers, Methuselah dies in the year of the flood. The usual Greek reading has him outlive it.
b: Adding the Masoretic numbers, Methuselah was 187 at Lamech's birth, Lamech 182 at Noah's, and Noah 600 at the flood: 187 + 182 + 600 = 969, the year Methuselah died. Jewish tradition said he died just before the flood, and that the seven days of 7:10 were days of mourning for him (Talmud, Sanhedrin 108b; Rashi on 7:10). In most Septuagint manuscripts, including the first hand of Codex Alexandrinus, Methuselah is 167 at Lamech's birth, which makes him die 14 years after the flood, though he was not on the ark. Augustine discussed this puzzle (City of God 15.11). Most scholars regard 167 as the original Greek and 187, found in a minority of Greek manuscripts and in Josephus, as a correction toward the Hebrew; Henry B. Smith Jr. argues the reverse. See the variant at 5:25.

a: This one will bring us relief
p: Lamech hears "comfort" (nacham) in Noah's name, which actually means "rest" (nuach).
b: The name Noach comes from the root nuach, "rest," but Lamech explains it with a similar-sounding verb, nacham, "comfort" or "relieve." The Septuagint, noticing, translated "this one will give us rest." The pun runs on: God will "regret" (nacham, 6:6–7) making humans, Noah will find favor (chen, the letters of his name reversed, 6:8), the ark will "rest" (8:4), and his sacrifice will be a "soothing" smell (nichoach, 8:21). "Painful labor" is the same word as in 3:17. Some see a fulfillment in Noah's vineyard (9:20), since wine brings relief (Psalm 104:15).

t: Who were the sons of God?
p: Angels, the godly line of Seth, or powerful rulers? Each view is ancient.
b: Angels: elsewhere "sons of God" are heavenly beings (Job 1:6; 38:7). This is the oldest known reading: 1 Enoch 6–11 tells of the Watchers, angels who came down and fathered giants; some Septuagint manuscripts read "angels of God"; Philo, Josephus (Antiquities 1.73) and most second-century Christian writers agree, and Jude 6–7 and 2 Peter 2:4 seem to allude to it. The line of Seth marrying the daughters of Cain: Julius Africanus, Augustine (City of God 15.23) and Chrysostom, followed by many Protestants; it avoids angels marrying (Matthew 22:30). Rulers: the Targums write "sons of the great ones," and Genesis Rabbah 26:5 reads "sons of judges"; tyrant kings took any women they wanted (Meredith Kline). Critical scholars mostly read divine beings, a fragment of an old myth about demigods.
r: Job 1:6; Job 38:7; Psalm 82:6; Jude 6–7; 2 Peter 2:4–5; 1 Peter 3:19–20; Matthew 22:30

a: My spirit will not stay in humans forever
t: 120 years: a lifespan or a countdown?
p: The verb is unclear, and so is the meaning of the 120 years.
b: The verb yadon appears only here. Ancient versions guessed "remain" (Septuagint, Vulgate); the KJV has "strive." The "spirit" is likely the breath of life God gave (2:7; 6:17). The 120 years are read two ways. A limit on human life: after the flood lifespans drop toward 120 (Moses dies at 120, Deuteronomy 34:7), though some later people live longer (11:10–25). A countdown to the flood: Targum Onkelos and Rashi say God gave the world 120 years to repent while Noah built the ark; 1 Peter 3:20 speaks of God's patience "in the days of Noah while the ark was being built." The phrase be-shaggam, "since," may also mean "in their going astray."

p: The word may mean "fallen ones." The Greek translated it "giants," and Numbers uses it for huge men.
b: Nefilim looks like it comes from nafal, "to fall": "fallen ones," or "ones who fall upon" others. The Septuagint wrote gigantes, "giants," and the KJV followed. The only other use is Numbers 13:33, where Israel's frightened spies report "Nephilim" in Canaan, beside whom they felt like grasshoppers. The verse does not say plainly that the Nephilim were the children of the sons of God; they were there "in those days, and later as well." "Heroes" is gibborim, warriors, the same word used for Nimrod (10:8). Ezekiel 32:27 speaks of fallen gibborim of old who went down to the grave with their weapons. Greek myth also told of half-divine heroes, and Gilgamesh was "two-thirds god."

p: Yetser, a "shaping" or plan, became the rabbinic word for the evil inclination.
b: Yetser machshevot libbo is literally "the shaping of the thoughts of his heart." Yetser comes from yatsar, the verb used when God "shaped" the man from dust (2:7): God shaped humans, and humans shape evil plans. The phrase returns after the flood, now as the reason God will be patient (8:21). From these verses the rabbis developed the idea of the yetser ha-ra, the evil inclination present in everyone, and the yetser ha-tov, the good inclination; the Torah is given as its remedy (Talmud, Kiddushin 30b). Christians often read these verses with Jeremiah 17:9 and Romans 3:10–18.

p: God is "sorry" and grieved. Yet 1 Samuel 15:29 says God is not a man, that he should change his mind.
b: The verb nicham means to feel sorrow and to change course. The same root gives Noah his explained name (5:29). "It pained him" uses the root of "pain" in 3:16–17: humans suffer pain, and so does God. Classical theism (Augustine, Aquinas, Calvin, Maimonides) holds that God does not change; such words describe God in human terms so that we grasp his real opposition to evil. Many modern theologians (Abraham Heschel on the divine pathos; Terence Fretheim) argue that the Bible means God truly feels and responds. Open theists go further and say God's knowledge of the future is open. All agree the text shows that sin wounds God and is not taken lightly. Compare 1 Samuel 15:11, 29, 35, where both statements stand in one chapter.
r: 1 Samuel 15:11; 1 Samuel 15:29; 1 Samuel 15:35; Numbers 23:19; Jeremiah 18:7–10; Jonah 3:10; Ephesians 4:30

a: But Noah found favor in the LORD's eyes.
p: In Hebrew, "favor" (chen) is Noah's name spelled backward.
b: Noach is spelled with the letters nun-chet (נח); chen, "favor" or "grace," is the same two letters reversed (חן). The KJV's "Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD" made this one of the best-known verses about grace. The order matters for many readers: Noah "found favor" before he is called righteous (6:9). Jewish and Christian readers both insist that God's favor and Noah's righteousness belong together (Ezekiel 14:14, 20; Hebrews 11:7).

a: he was blameless in his generations
p: "In his generations": was Noah righteous only by comparison, or righteous even in such a time?
b: Tamim, "whole" or "blameless," is the word for an animal without defect (Leviticus 1:3) and for Abraham's calling (17:1). "In his generations" puzzled the rabbis. The Talmud records two views (Sanhedrin 108a; Rashi): Rabbi Yochanan said Noah was righteous only by the standard of his wicked age, and in Abraham's day he would have counted for nothing; Resh Lakish said that if he was righteous even in such an age, how much greater he would have been in a better one. Christians remember him as "a preacher of righteousness" (2 Peter 2:5) and an heir of righteousness by faith (Hebrews 11:7).

p: The same verb comes four times in three verses: the earth was ruined, so God will ruin it.
b: Shachat means to spoil or corrupt, and also to destroy. The earth "had gone to ruin" (6:11), "there it was, ruined" (6:12), "all flesh had ruined its way" (6:12), and God says "I am going to ruin them" (6:13, 17). The flood is pictured as God completing what people had already done to the world. "Violence" (chamas) is lawless brutality, often against the weak (Amos 3:10; Ezekiel 7:23). Jesus compares the last days to "the days of Noah" (Matthew 24:37–39).

t: An ark: a box, not a ship
p: The Hebrew tevah is the word for baby Moses' basket. Gopher wood is unknown.
b: Tevah appears only for Noah's ark and the basket in which Moses floated on the Nile (Exodus 2:3, 5), both coated with pitch and both saving a life through water. It may be an Egyptian loanword for a chest or box. The ark has no sail, oar or rudder; its course is in God's hands. "Gopher wood" (gofer) is found nowhere else; cypress and pine are guesses. "Pitch" (kofer) is bitumen, also used for the boat in the Babylonian flood story; the verb "coat" (kafar) is from the same root as the Hebrew for "atonement," a link many preachers have drawn, though the meanings are distinct.

p: About 450 feet long, 75 feet wide and 45 feet high. The Babylonian ark was a cube or a round boat.
b: A cubit was the length from elbow to fingertip, about 18 inches, so the ark was roughly 450 by 75 by 45 feet, a box with a 6 to 1 ratio of length to width. Young-earth writers point out that such a shape is very stable, citing ship-design studies, and that the volume could hold the animals of each "kind." Critics answer that no wooden ship of that size is known to have been seaworthy. In the Epic of Gilgamesh, Utnapishtim's boat is a cube, about 120 cubits on each side, in seven stories. An Old Babylonian tablet published by Irving Finkel (2014) describes the flood boat as a huge round coracle of rope and reeds. Genesis's proportions are the most ship-like of the three.

p: The word tsohar is found only here. It may mean a roof, a window or an opening for light.
b: Tsohar is related to tsohorayim, "noon," so many older translations (KJV "window") took it as an opening for light; others relate it to an Arabic word for "back" or "top" and read "roof." The phrase "finishing it off a cubit above" suggests a gap for light and air under the roof. Genesis Rabbah 31:11 records a view that it was a glowing jewel that lit the ark. The "window" Noah opens in 8:6 is a different word (challon).

a: with you I will set up my covenant
p: Berit, "covenant," first appears here: a binding promise. Its full form comes in 9:8–17.
b: A berit is a solemn agreement that binds parties together, sealed with an oath or a sign. This is the first use of the word in the Bible. "Set up" (heqim) usually means to confirm or keep a covenant, and some scholars (William Dumbrell) argue that God is reaffirming a commitment already made at creation; most read it as a promise of the covenant described after the flood (9:9–17). Later covenants follow: with Abraham (15:18; 17:2), with Israel at Sinai (Exodus 24:8), with David (2 Samuel 7; Psalm 89:3), and the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31–34; Luke 22:20).

a: He did everything just as God commanded him.
p: Noah never speaks in the flood story. He simply obeys.
b: Noah says nothing from 5:29 to 9:25. The narrator says four times that he did what God commanded (6:22; 7:5, 9, 16). The same phrase describes Moses and Israel building the tabernacle (Exodus 39:32, 42–43; 40:16), and many scholars see a deliberate link: both builders make a God-designed structure that preserves life in God's presence. Hebrews 11:7 calls Noah's building an act of faith, "warned about things not yet seen."

p: 6:19 says two of every kind; 7:2 says seven of the clean animals. One account or two?
b: The Hebrew "seven seven" can mean seven pairs or seven animals (three pairs and one extra for sacrifice, 8:20); the rabbis and modern scholars are divided. Critical scholars see two sources woven together: the Priestly account ("God," two of each, 6:19–20; 7:15–16) and the Yahwist ("the LORD," seven of the clean, 7:1–3), which also differ on the flood's length (40 days, 7:17, or 150, 7:24). Traditional readers answer that 6:19 is the general command and 7:2 adds detail, so that there would be animals to offer (8:20) and to eat (9:3), and that the numbers of days fit one calendar (see the chapter page). The clean-unclean distinction later appears in Leviticus 11, but this verse assumes it was already known.

p: Forty is the Bible's number for a full time of testing or waiting.
b: Moses was on the mountain forty days and nights (Exodus 24:18; 34:28), Israel wandered forty years (Numbers 14:33–34), Elijah walked forty days to Horeb (1 Kings 19:8), Nineveh had forty days to repent (Jonah 3:4), and Jesus fasted forty days in the wilderness (Matthew 4:2). Noah also waits forty days before opening the window (8:6). The number marks a complete period, often of trial before a new beginning. It may also be a round number for "a long time," as in many ancient texts.
r: 8:6; Exodus 24:18; Numbers 14:33–34; 1 Kings 19:8; Jonah 3:4; Matthew 4:1–2; Acts 1:3

p: The rabbis asked why God waited seven more days. Their answer: to mourn the righteous Methuselah.
b: God had said "after seven more days" (7:4). The Talmud (Sanhedrin 108b) and Rashi explain the delay as the seven days of mourning for Methuselah, who by the Hebrew numbers died in the year of the flood (see the note at 5:27), so that the world would honor a righteous man before judgment came. Another view in the same passage: God gave the world one last week to repent. Seven-day periods recur in the story (7:4, 10; 8:10, 12), echoing the week of creation.

a: in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month
