p: The flood is dated to the day by Noah's age, like an official chronicle.
b: The flood story gives exact dates: it begins on 2/17 of Noah's 600th year (7:11), the ark rests on 7/17 (8:4), mountaintops appear on 10/1 (8:5), the waters dry on 1/1 of the 601st year (8:13), and the earth is dry on 2/27 (8:14), a year and ten days later. The rabbis argued over which month came first. Rabbi Eliezer said the second month was Marheshvan, in the autumn; Rabbi Joshua said it was Iyar, in the spring (Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 11b). Some scholars note that a lunar year of 354 days plus 11 equals a solar year of 365. The Septuagint dates the start and the landing to the 27th (see the variant), so its flood lasts exactly one year, and Jubilees and the Qumran Commentary on Genesis A (4Q252) rework the dates for a 364-day calendar. Gordon Wenham showed that the dates and numbers form a mirror pattern centered on 8:1.

a: all the springs of the great deep burst open, and the windows of the sky were opened
p: The waters God separated in 1:6–9 rush back together. The flood is creation run backward.
b: On day two God divided the waters above from the waters below, and on day three he gathered the waters so dry land could appear (1:6–10). Now the "great deep" (tehom, 1:2) bursts up from below and the "windows" (floodgates) of the sky open from above, and the earth returns toward the watery chaos of 1:2. After the flood, a wind passes over the waters (8:1, compare 1:2), dry land appears (8:13), and the creation blessing is repeated (9:1). Many scholars (David Clines) read the whole flood as uncreation and re-creation. Young-earth geologists read the verse physically: "catastrophic plate tectonics" (Baumgardner, Austin and others, 1994) proposes that the fountains of the deep were huge eruptions of water and rock.

a: Then the LORD shut the door behind him
p: In the Babylonian story the hero seals his own boat. Here the LORD does it.
b: In Gilgamesh Tablet XI Utnapishtim goes into his boat and closes the door himself. Genesis says the LORD shut Noah in, with his own hand, as it were. The verse uses both "God" and "the LORD": "as God had commanded him. Then the LORD shut the door." Source critics assign the two names to two sources; others see a shift from God the Creator giving orders to the LORD, the covenant God, protecting his own. Jesus' parable of the shut door may echo the scene (Matthew 25:10; Luke 13:25).

a: all the high mountains under the whole sky were covered
t: A worldwide or a regional flood?
p: Was the flood global, regional, or a story built on a Mesopotamian memory? Each view has serious defenders.
b: Global (traditional, young-earth creationists): "all the high mountains under the whole sky" and the death of all life outside the ark (7:21–23) mean a worldwide flood, which laid down most of the rock layers; 2 Peter 3:6 says the world "was flooded and destroyed." Regional (many old-earth evangelicals: Hugh Ross, Davis Young; earlier, John Pye Smith in 1839): "the whole earth" (kol ha-arets) can mean "the whole land" or the known world (41:57), and a vast flood in Mesopotamia wiped out the human world of that time. Critical: the story retells a Mesopotamian tradition (see 8:8, 8:21) for new purposes. Geologists treat it as consensus that there was no single worldwide flood in human history. Proposed local floods include flood layers at Ur, Shuruppak and Kish (not all from the same time) and the Black Sea theory of William Ryan and Walter Pitman (1998).

p: About 22 feet, exactly half the ark's height of thirty cubits.
b: Fifteen cubits is half the ark's height (6:15). Many commentators think the writer means that the ark, sinking about half its height into the water, never ran aground until the waters fell (8:4). Others take it as simply the depth over the highest peaks. Regional-flood readers suggest it is how deep the water was over the hills of the region the writer knew.

t: How long did the flood last?
p: Forty days of rain, 150 days of high water, about a year in all.
b: The rain falls forty days (7:12, 17); the waters "held the upper hand" for 150 days (7:24; 8:3), and the ark rests five months after the start (8:4). Noah leaves the ark after a year and about ten days (7:11; 8:14). Critical scholars see two counts from two sources (40 days in J, 150 in P). Others read one timeline: the forty days are part of the 150. The Babylonian stories are far shorter: the storm lasts six days and six nights in Gilgamesh (the second number is broken on the tablet and restored), and seven days and seven nights in the Sumerian flood story of Ziusudra.

p: To remember, in Hebrew, is to act for someone. This verse is the turning point of the flood story.
b: Zakhar does not mean God had forgotten. When God remembers, he acts on a promise: he remembers his covenant and rescues Israel from Egypt (Exodus 2:24), and he remembers Hannah and she conceives (1 Samuel 1:19). Gordon Wenham showed that the flood story is built as a mirror, with numbers and events going up to this verse and back down after it; "God remembered Noah" stands at the center. God remembers "the animals" too. Then a "wind" (ruach) passes over the waters, as God's ruach moved over the waters at creation (1:2).

p: Ararat is the land of Urartu, in eastern Turkey and Armenia. The text says "mountains," not one peak.
b: Ararat is the Hebrew form of Urartu, a kingdom of the 800s to 600s BC around Lake Van, known from Assyrian records (compare 2 Kings 19:37; Jeremiah 51:27). The text names a mountain region, not the 16,854-foot peak now called Mount Ararat, a name given to it much later. Other traditions put the landing in the mountains of Kurdistan: Berossus and the Targums say "Qardu" (the Gordyene mountains), and the Qur'an names Mount Judi (11:44). In Gilgamesh the boat lands on Mount Nimush (once read Nisir). Many expeditions have searched for the ark; no find has convinced scientists or most archaeologists. "Came to rest" (vattanach) plays on Noah's name.

a: Then he sent the dove out from him
p: The Babylonian flood hero also sends out a dove, a swallow and a raven. This parallel is clear.
b: In Gilgamesh Tablet XI, when the boat grounds on Mount Nimush, Utnapishtim waits seven days, then sends out a dove, which finds no resting place and comes back; then a swallow, which also returns; then a raven, which finds the waters receding, eats, and does not return. Nearly all scholars agree that Genesis and Gilgamesh XI share a tradition; most critical scholars think Genesis depends on it, directly or indirectly; many conservatives think both descend from a common memory. The differences are telling: Genesis has a raven first, then the dove three times, and a fresh olive leaf as the sign of new life.

t: The dove and the olive leaf
p: The leaf shows that trees are growing again on lower ground. It became a worldwide sign of peace.
b: Olive trees do not grow high on mountains, so a fresh leaf means the water has gone down to the hills and valleys. The rabbis said the dove brought it from the Mount of Olives, or from the garden of Eden (Genesis Rabbah 33:6), and that the dove was saying "better bitter food from God's hand than sweet food from man's" (Talmud, Eruvin 18b). Christians linked the dove with the Holy Spirit descending on Jesus after his baptism in water (Matthew 3:16), and 1 Peter 3:20–21 links the flood with baptism. The dove with an olive branch became a common sign of peace.

a: in the first month, on the first of the month
t: A new year, a new world
p: The earth is uncovered on New Year's Day. Creation starts again.
b: The waters dry on the first day of the first month of Noah's 601st year: the world begins again on a New Year's Day. Moses will raise the tabernacle on the same date (Exodus 40:2, 17), and Hezekiah begins cleansing the temple on it (2 Chronicles 29:17). "The face of the ground, drying" echoes the dry ground of 1:9. From here the story repeats creation: the animals "swarm" and "grow many" (8:17; 1:22), God blesses humans (9:1; 1:28), and he gives them food (9:3; 1:29).

a: Noah built an altar to the LORD
p: This is the first altar named in the Bible, and the first whole burnt offering.
b: An olah, "whole burnt offering" (literally "what goes up"), was burned entirely on the altar as a gift to God; Leviticus 1 sets out the rite. Noah offers only clean animals, which explains the extra clean animals of 7:2. Later Abraham (12:7–8; 22:9), Isaac (26:25), Jacob (35:7) and Moses (Exodus 17:15) build altars in the same way at turning points. Christian readers have seen in Noah's offering, made by the one man through whom the world is saved, a picture of Christ's self-offering "as a fragrant offering" (Ephesians 5:2).

a: The LORD smelled the soothing smell
p: In Gilgamesh the hungry gods crowd around the sacrifice. The contrast with Genesis is sharp.
b: In Gilgamesh XI, Utnapishtim offers a sacrifice on the mountain, and "the gods smelled the savor, the gods smelled the sweet savor, the gods gathered like flies over the sacrificer." In Atrahasis the gods had gone hungry during the flood, with no humans to feed them. Genesis keeps the picture of God smelling the offering, a phrase that becomes standard in the Law (reach nichoach, Leviticus 1:9, 13, 17), but God is not hungry. He accepts the offering and makes a promise. Nichoach, "soothing," is another play on Noah's name (5:29).

a: what the human heart shapes is evil from youth on
t: The same reason, now for mercy
p: The evil of the human heart was the reason for the flood (6:5). Now it is the reason for patience.
b: The words repeat 6:5 (yetser lev ha-adam, "the shaping of the human heart"). Before the flood, human evil was why God judged; after it, the same evil is why God promises not to destroy again. The flood did not change the human heart. The conjunction ki can mean "because" or "although"; many translations write "even though," and the Plain English Translation "though." Either way, God's patience now rests on his own promise, not on human goodness. Jewish tradition took "from youth" to mean that the evil inclination is present from birth, while the good inclination comes with maturity (Avot de-Rabbi Natan 16).
orig: כִּי יֵצֶר לֵב הָאָדָם רַע מִנְּעֻרָיו (ki yetser lev ha-adam ra mi-ne'urav)

a: seedtime and harvest, cold and heat
p: God's promise that the seasons will keep turning becomes a picture of his faithfulness.
b: The short poem lists four pairs. Jeremiah points to God's covenant with "day and night" as proof that his covenant with David and Israel will not fail (Jeremiah 33:20–21, 25–26; 31:35–36). Paul tells the people of Lystra that God "gave you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons" as a witness to himself (Acts 14:17). "As long as the earth lasts" hints that the earth itself will not last forever (Isaiah 51:6; 2 Peter 3:10).

a: Everything that creeps and lives is yours for food
p: After the flood God permits meat, which 1:29 did not. Readers explain the change differently.
b: In 1:29–30 God gives plants for food; now he gives "everything," with one limit (9:4). Many readers, Jewish and Christian, hold that people were vegetarian before the flood. Rashi says so; young-earth creationists add that animals were too. Some old-earth readers say 1:29 does not forbid meat but simply lists what God provided. The fear of humans that falls on animals (9:2) suggests that peace between humans and animals has broken down. The prophets look toward its return (Isaiah 11:6–9; Hosea 2:18). Paul says all foods are clean when received with thanks (1 Timothy 4:3–5; Romans 14:20).

a: flesh with its life, its blood, you must not eat
p: The rabbis built the seven laws of Noah partly on this chapter, and the early church kept the ban on blood.
b: Since all people descend from Noah, the rabbis held that God's commands here bind every nation. The Talmud lists seven "laws of the children of Noah": to set up courts of justice, and not to blaspheme, worship idols, commit sexual sin, murder, steal, or eat a limb torn from a living animal (Sanhedrin 56a–b). A Gentile who keeps them is counted righteous. The blood ban rests on the idea that "the life is in the blood" and belongs to God (Leviticus 17:10–14). When the church in Jerusalem welcomed Gentile believers, it asked them to abstain from blood and from strangled animals (Acts 15:20, 29), which many scholars connect with this Noahic tradition.

a: by a human his blood will be spilled,
p: The Hebrew is six words that mirror each other: blood for blood. "By a human" may also mean "in a human."
b: Shofekh dam ha-adam / ba-adam damo yishafekh: "one who sheds / blood / of the human // by the human / his blood / will be shed." The form itself shows the punishment fitting the crime. Ba-adam usually means "by a human," that is, by human justice. The rabbis also read it "within a human": Rabbi Ishmael said this means one who kills a person inside a person, a child in the womb (Talmud, Sanhedrin 57b). The reason given is the image of God (1:26–27): murder attacks God's own likeness. James 3:9 uses the same reason to forbid even cursing a person.
orig: שֹׁפֵךְ דַּם הָאָדָם בָּאָדָם דָּמוֹ יִשָּׁפֵךְ

t: Does this command the death penalty?
p: Christians and Jews have read this verse as a basis for capital punishment, as a warning, and as a description.
b: A permanent command: many Christian writers (Luther, Calvin and many Reformed and Lutheran theologians) and some modern evangelicals read it as God giving human government the duty to punish murder with death, before and apart from the Law of Moses (compare Romans 13:4). A principle of justice: Jewish law made it very hard to carry out a death sentence, and the Mishnah says a court that executed one person in seven years (or seventy) was called destructive (Mishnah Makkot 1:10). A warning or description: some read "his blood will be shed" as what happens, not what must be done (compare Matthew 26:52). The Catholic Church, which long allowed the death penalty, revised its Catechism in 2018 to call it "inadmissible" (CCC 2267). Opponents of the death penalty also appeal to the image of God, which the murderer still bears (4:15).

a: I am setting up my covenant with you
p: God's first covenant includes all people and all animals, and asks nothing of them in return.
b: The word "covenant" comes seven times in 9:9–17. This covenant is made with Noah, his descendants (that is, all humanity) and "every living creature," even "the earth" (9:13). It is one-sided: God binds himself, and its sign is in the sky, not on human bodies. It is called a covenant "that lasts forever" (berit olam, 9:16). Isaiah 54:9–10 compares God's oath to Noah with his oath never to abandon Israel. Isaiah 24:5 may echo it when it says the earth's people "have broken the everlasting covenant." Hosea 2:18 promises a new covenant with the animals.

a: my bow I have put in the clouds
p: The Hebrew word for rainbow is the word for a war bow. Many readers see God setting his weapon aside.
b: Qeshet is the ordinary word for an archer's bow; the Bible never uses a separate word for "rainbow." Elsewhere God shoots arrows of lightning from his bow (Psalm 7:12–13; Habakkuk 3:9–11). Many scholars read the image as God hanging up his weapon, pointed away from the earth, as a sign of peace. In the Babylonian Enuma Elish, Marduk's bow is set in the sky as a star after his victory (Tablet VI). The rainbow returns around God's throne (Ezekiel 1:28; Revelation 4:3; 10:1). Did rainbows exist before this? Young-earth writers who think there was no rain before the flood (2:5) say no; most readers think an existing sight was given a new meaning.

a: was the first to plant a vineyard
p: The Hebrew can mean "Noah began" or "Noah was the first." Wine is a blessing that can be abused.
b: Vayyachel means "he began." It may mean that Noah was the first to plant a vineyard, or simply that he "began to farm" again after the flood ("a man of the ground" can mean "a farmer"). Lamech had hoped Noah would bring "relief" from the cursed ground (5:29), and wine "gladdens human hearts" (Psalm 104:15; Judges 9:13). But the first mention of wine also shows its danger. The rabbis noted that the same verb, vayyachel, can mean "was profaned": by planting a vineyard first, Noah "made himself common" (Genesis Rabbah 36:3).

a: saw the nakedness of his father
p: Was Ham's sin only looking? The rabbis and modern scholars suggest something worse.
b: He looked and mocked: the plain sense is that Ham saw his father exposed and told others, instead of covering him as his brothers did; honoring parents included protecting their dignity (Exodus 20:12). Many Jewish and Christian readers take this view. A sexual act: in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 70a) Rav and Shmuel disagree whether Ham castrated or sexually abused Noah, since Noah "found out what his youngest son had done to him" (9:24). Incest with Noah's wife: in Leviticus 18:7–8, "the nakedness of your father's wife" is called "your father's nakedness," so to expose it means to have sex with your father's wife. John Bergsma and Scott Hahn (2005) argued that Ham did this and that Canaan was born from it, which would explain why Canaan is cursed. Most commentators still prefer the plain sense.

p: Ham is listed in the middle of the three brothers, yet he is called "the youngest."
b: Beno ha-qatan means "his young" or "his youngest son." Shem, Ham and Japheth may be listed in an order of importance, not birth, so Ham could be the youngest. Some ancient and modern readers think the "son" is Noah's grandson Canaan, which would explain why Canaan, and not Ham, is cursed. Others read qatan as "lesser" or "worthless."

t: The curse was on Canaan, not Ham or Africa
p: This verse was misused for centuries to justify enslaving Africans. The text curses only Canaan.
b: Noah curses Canaan, Ham's son, not Ham, and the Canaanites lived in the land later promised to Israel (10:15–19), not in Africa. Critical scholars read the verse as explaining Israel's later rule over the Canaanites (Joshua 9:23; 1 Kings 9:20–21). Traditional readers see a prophecy, with judgment falling on Canaanite sin (Leviticus 18:24–28). The idea of a "curse of Ham" on Black Africans grew up in late antiquity and the Middle Ages, and was used in the Islamic world and later in Europe and America to defend slavery and segregation. Historians such as David Goldenberg (The Curse of Ham, 2003) and Stephen Haynes (Noah's Curse, 2002) have traced it. Nearly all churches and scholars today reject it as a misreading.

a: May God make room for Japheth,
t: Japheth in the tents of Shem
p: "Make room" (yaft) plays on Japheth's name. The rabbis read this verse as permission to translate the Torah into Greek.
b: Yaft le-Yefet, "may he enlarge Japheth," is a pun on the name. Who lives in Shem's tents? God: Targum Onkelos says God will make his presence (the Shekhinah) dwell in the tents of Shem, that is, in Israel's sanctuary. Japheth: Japheth's descendants include the Greeks (Javan, 10:2), and the Talmud links yaft with yafeh, "beautiful," reading the verse as: "let the beauty of Japheth be in the tents of Shem," so the Torah may be written in Greek (Megillah 9b). Many Christians read it as the Gentile nations sharing in Israel's blessing (Ephesians 2:11–22).

a: This is the family history of Noah's sons
p: Chapter 10 maps the world Israel knew as one family. It counts seventy names.
b: The chapter lists the peoples descended from Noah's three sons: Japheth's to the north and west (Anatolia, the Aegean, the Caucasus), Ham's to the south and southwest (Egypt, Africa, Canaan, Mesopotamian Babylon), Shem's to the east (Elam, Assyria, Aram, Arabia). The Hebrew list has seventy names (the Septuagint has a few more), and Jewish tradition speaks of "seventy nations" (compare Deuteronomy 32:8). Many entries are peoples or places, not single people: "the Jebusites," "Mizraim" (Egypt). The groups follow geography and politics as much as language: Canaan is placed under Ham, though the Canaanites spoke a Semitic language close to Hebrew. No other ancient text gives such a complete map of humanity as one family.

p: Javan is Greece and Madai is the Medes. Magog, Meshech and Tubal return in Ezekiel and Revelation.
b: Javan is Ionia, the Greeks (Daniel 8:21 has "the king of Javan," Greece). Madai is the Medes of Iran. Gomer is usually taken as the Cimmerians, and Tubal and Meshech as peoples of eastern Anatolia known to the Assyrians as Tabal and Mushki. Magog is unknown; Josephus thought of the Scythians. Ezekiel's prophecy names "Gog, of the land of Magog, chief prince of Meshech and Tubal" as the enemy from the far north (Ezekiel 38:2–3), and Revelation 20:8 turns "Gog and Magog" into the nations at the end of history.

p: A northern people near Ararat. In the Middle Ages the name came to mean Germany.
b: Jeremiah 51:27 calls on "Ararat, Minni and Ashkenaz" to attack Babylon, and many scholars link Ashkenaz with the Scythians (Assyrian Ishkuzai). In medieval Hebrew, Ashkenaz became the name for Germany, and Jews of central and eastern Europe came to be called Ashkenazim. In the same way, Sepharad (Obadiah 20) came to mean Spain, home of the Sephardim.

p: Tarshish was a far western port; Kittim was Cyprus, later a code name for Greeks and Romans.
b: Tarshish was famous for its ships and metals (1 Kings 10:22; Ezekiel 27:12), and it was where Jonah tried to flee (Jonah 1:3). It may be Tartessos in Spain, or a place in Sardinia or Cilicia. The Kittim are the people of Kition on Cyprus. In later texts the name stretched to Greeks (1 Maccabees 1:1) and Romans (Daniel 11:30), and in the Dead Sea Scrolls the "Kittim" are the enemy power of the last days, usually understood as Rome.
r: Jonah 1:3; 1 Kings 10:22; Ezekiel 27:12; Isaiah 23:1; Daniel 11:30; Numbers 24:24

p: Chapter 10 has many languages; chapter 11 begins with one. Are the chapters out of order?
b: 10:5, 20 and 31 say the nations spread out "each with its own language," but 11:1 begins with the whole earth speaking one language. Most readers think chapter 10 runs ahead to show the result, and chapter 11 then goes back to tell how it happened, which is common in Hebrew storytelling. Genesis often finishes one line before returning to the main thread (compare 25:12–18 before 25:19). Critical scholars see two traditions about the spread of peoples, one peaceful (chapter 10, a blessing fulfilled, 9:1) and one a judgment (11:1–9), placed side by side.

p: Cush is Nubia, Mizraim is Egypt, Put is probably Libya, and Canaan the land of Canaan.
b: Cush is the kingdom south of Egypt, in modern Sudan (the Greek "Ethiopia"), though 10:7–8 may also use the name for peoples of Arabia and Mesopotamia. Mitsrayim is the Hebrew name for Egypt, still used in Hebrew and Arabic (Misr). Put is probably Libya. Canaan is placed with Egypt, perhaps because Egypt ruled Canaan for much of the late Bronze Age (about 1550 to 1150 BC). The list describes peoples by geography and history, not by skin color or race; race in the modern sense is foreign to the text.

p: The first empire-builder. Scholars have suggested several Mesopotamian kings and gods.
b: Nimrod is the first "hero" (gibbor, the word for the mighty men of 6:4) and the first to rule a kingdom, in Babylonia and then Assyria. No Mesopotamian king of that name is known. Proposals include Sargon of Akkad (about 2300 BC), who founded the first empire; Naram-Sin, his grandson; Tukulti-Ninurta I of Assyria (about 1240 BC; E. A. Speiser's suggestion); Gilgamesh; and the war and hunting god Ninurta, after whom the Assyrian city of Nimrud is named today. Micah 5:6 calls Assyria "the land of Nimrod." Many readers hear in the name the Hebrew marad, "to rebel."

a: a hero of the hunt in the LORD's sight
p: Literally "before the LORD": perhaps praise. Jewish tradition read it as defiance and made Nimrod the builder of Babel.
b: The Hebrew "before the LORD" can mean "in the LORD's sight," as the Plain English Translation has it, or simply "the greatest," like "a city great in God's eyes" (Jonah 3:3). Assyrian kings boasted of their hunts, and the saying may be praise. But Jewish tradition read Nimrod as a rebel. Josephus says Nimrod urged people to build the tower to defy God (Antiquities 1.113–119), and the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan calls him "mighty in sin before the LORD." Later legends made him the king who threw Abraham into a furnace (see 11:28). Genesis itself does not link Nimrod to the tower, though both stories begin in "the land of Shinar" (10:10; 11:2).

p: Babel is Babylon, Erech is Uruk, and Akkad is Sargon's capital. Calneh is unknown.
b: Babel is the Hebrew name of Babylon. Erech is Uruk (modern Warka in Iraq), one of the first true cities in the world, where some of the earliest writing has been found (about 3200 BC); it was the city of Gilgamesh. Akkad (Agade) was the capital of Sargon's empire, its site still not found. Calneh is unknown; some scholars repoint the Hebrew to read kullanah, "all of them," giving "Babel, Erech and Akkad, all of them in the land of Shinar." Shinar is the Bible's name for Babylonia (Daniel 1:2; Zechariah 5:11).

a: From that land he went out to Assyria
p: The Hebrew can mean "he went to Assyria" or "Asshur went out."
b: Hebrew can read yatsa Ashshur as "he went out to Asshur" (Assyria) or "Asshur went out." The KJV took Asshur as the subject, a son of Shem (10:22) who founded Nineveh. Most modern versions make Nimrod the subject, since Micah 5:6 links "the land of Assyria" and "the land of Nimrod." Nineveh, near modern Mosul, and Calah (Kalhu, modern Nimrud) were royal cities of Assyria, both excavated since the 1800s. "The great city" may be Calah, or Nineveh, which Jonah calls "that great city" (Jonah 1:2).

p: Other passages say the Philistines came from Caphtor, probably Crete.
b: Amos 9:7 and Jeremiah 47:4 say the Philistines came from Caphtor, which most scholars identify with Crete (Egyptian Keftiu). The phrase here may originally have stood after "the Caphtorim," or the Philistines may have had more than one origin. Archaeology connects the Philistines with the "Sea Peoples" who came from the Aegean world and settled the coast of Canaan about 1175 BC.

a: He was the ancestor of all the sons of Eber
p: Eber's name sounds like Ivri, "Hebrew." The verse singles out the line that leads to Abraham.
b: Shem is called "the ancestor of all the sons of Eber" before his own sons are listed, which marks Eber as important. The word Ivri, "Hebrew," first used for Abram (14:13), looks like it comes from Eber's name, or from avar, "to cross over": the people from "across" the river (Joshua 24:2–3). "Sons of Eber" may include more peoples than Israel alone. The last phrase is ambiguous: Shem may be "the older brother of Japheth" or "the brother of Japheth the elder."

a: Peleg, for in his days the earth was split up
p: Peleg means "division." The text does not say what was divided.
b: Peleg is linked with niflegah, "was divided." The scattering at Babel: most Jewish and Christian readers take it as the division of peoples and languages in chapter 11 (Rashi). Division of land: some read a division of territory among the clans (Jubilees 8:8–11; compare Deuteronomy 32:8). Canals: peleg also means a water channel (Psalm 1:3), and some scholars think of the irrigation canals that split up Mesopotamia. Continents: a few modern readers see continental drift, but nearly all scholars, including most young-earth creationists, reject this.

p: Joktan's sons are mostly tribes of south Arabia: Sheba, Ophir, Hazarmaveth.
b: Many of Joktan's sons are names of places in Arabia. Hazarmaveth is Hadramaut, a region of Yemen still called by that name. Sheba is the kingdom of Saba in Yemen, whose queen visited Solomon (1 Kings 10:1). Ophir was famous for its gold (1 Kings 9:28; Job 22:24), probably on the Arabian or East African coast. Havilah also appears in the Eden story (2:11), and two Shebas and two Havilahs appear in the lists (10:7), showing how complex the ancient peoples' ties were.

p: A Sumerian poem also looks back to a time when all lands praised one god in one tongue.
b: In the Sumerian epic Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta (copies from about 2000 to 1700 BC) there is a passage, called the spell of Nudimmud, that speaks of a time when "the whole universe, the people in unison" praised the god Enlil "in one tongue," and of the god Enki changing their speech. Samuel Noah Kramer first drew attention to it. Scholars still argue whether it looks back to a lost unity or forward to a hoped-for one, and how the confusion happened. It is a real parallel in idea, but the plot is very different, and there is no tower.

a: one language and one set of words
p: What was the first language? Readers took the story as history, as a story about empire, or as an origin tale.
b: A literal first language: Jewish tradition held that it was Hebrew, "the holy tongue" (the Targums; Rashi), and some church fathers agreed; others proposed Aramaic or Syriac. A story about empire: many scholars (and some conservatives) note that Assyrian kings boasted of making conquered peoples "of one mouth," and read "one language" as imperial uniformity. An origin tale: critical scholars read it as an explanation of why humans speak many languages. Linguists hold that languages have diversified over tens of thousands of years, and the oldest written languages (Sumerian, Egyptian) already differed greatly by 3000 BC. The phrase "one set of words" (devarim achadim) may mean one vocabulary, or one purpose.
orig: שָׂפָה אֶחָת וּדְבָרִים אֲחָדִים (safah achat u-devarim achadim)

p: The Hebrew miqqedem can mean "from the east," "eastward" or "in the east."
b: The KJV has "as they journeyed from the east"; many modern versions have "eastward" or "in the east." Moving east has a pattern in Genesis: the man is driven out east of Eden (3:24), Cain settles east of Eden (4:16), and Lot goes east toward Sodom (13:11). Shinar, the land of Babylon (10:10), lies in the broad plain between the Tigris and Euphrates. "Valley" (biq'ah) means a wide, flat plain.

a: They had brick to use as stone and bitumen to use as mortar
p: The narrator explains Babylonian building to readers in a land of stone. The Hebrew is full of sound-play.
b: In the hills of Israel people built with stone and lime mortar. Mesopotamia has almost no stone, so it built with mud brick, fired brick for important buildings, and bitumen (natural asphalt) as mortar. Archaeologists have found baked bricks set in bitumen in the ziggurats of Ur and Babylon. The Hebrew piles up sounds: nilbenah levenim, "let's brick bricks" (the Plain English Translation "mold bricks"), ve-nisrefah lisrefah, "and burn them to a burning," and the pair chemar (bitumen) and chomer (mortar). Many hear mockery: these people make with their own hands what God gave freely.
orig: הַלְּבֵנָה לְאָבֶן וְהַחֵמָר ... לַחֹמֶר (ha-levenah le-aven ve-ha-chemar... la-chomer)

a: a tower with its head in the heavens
p: Babylon's temple tower Etemenanki, "House of the Foundation of Heaven and Earth," fits the picture.
b: A Mesopotamian ziggurat was a stepped tower of brick with a shrine on top, thought to link heaven and earth, a stairway for the god to come down. The great ziggurat of Babylon was called Etemenanki, "House of the Foundation of Heaven and Earth," beside Marduk's temple Esagila, "House whose Head is High." In the Enuma Elish (Tablet VI) the gods build Esagila for Marduk and raise its head on high. Nebuchadnezzar II (604–562 BC) boasted of making the tower's top "rival the heavens." Greek visitors described it (Herodotus 1.181). The phrase "in the heavens" can also be ordinary boasting (Deuteronomy 1:28). Etemenanki in its known form is later than the setting of Genesis 11, but older ziggurats stood in many cities.

a: We will win a name for ourselves
p: Pride, refusal to scatter, or the rise of empire? The text gives hints, not a verdict.
b: Pride: they want "a name," as the heroes of 6:4 were "men of a name." In the next chapter God promises Abram, "I will bless you and make your name great" (12:2): a name is God's gift, not a human achievement. Shem's own name means "Name." Refusing to scatter: God told humans to "fill the earth" (1:28; 9:1); they build so that they will not be scattered. Empire: a city built by forced labor in Nimrod's land, where uniformity serves power (many modern scholars, and some Jewish interpreters who read "one set of words" as one command). Reaching heaven: Josephus and the rabbis imagined a war against God (Talmud, Sanhedrin 109a). Christians often set Babel beside Pentecost.

a: The LORD came down to see
p: The tower meant to reach heaven is so small that God must come down to see it.
b: The humor is plain: the builders reach for the sky, and the LORD has to "come down" to look at what they made. The rabbis drew a lesson for judges: even God, who knows everything, "came down to see" before acting, so a judge must not condemn before seeing the facts (Rashi, from Genesis Rabbah 38:9; compare 18:21). "The human race" is literally "the sons of the human" (benei ha-adam), a reminder that they are made from dust (2:7).

p: The builders said "Come, let's" twice. God answers with his own "Come, let us."
b: The builders say havah, "come," in 11:3 and 11:4: "Come on, let's mold bricks," "Come on, let's build." God answers with the same word: "Come, let us go down." The plural "us" returns from 1:26 and 3:22 (see the note on 1:26). "Mix up" (navlah, from balal) is the sound-play that will explain the name Babel in 11:9. The words "so that no one will understand" are literally "will not hear": the problem is not sound but sense.

a: That is how the place got the name Babel
p: In Babylon's own language the name meant "gate of god." Genesis hears "confusion."
b: Babylonians explained their city's name as Bab-ili, "gate of god." Genesis connects it with Hebrew balal, "to mix up" or "confuse." Most scholars see a deliberate counter-explanation: the city that called itself the gate to heaven is really the place of confusion. The English word "babble" is not from "Babel" (it is an imitation of baby talk), though the two have been linked in popular thought. Later Scripture makes Babylon the great enemy city, from Daniel to "Babylon the great" in Revelation 17–18.

a: the LORD mixed up the speech of all the earth
p: At Pentecost the Spirit lets people of many languages hear one message. Christians read it as Babel reversed.
b: At Pentecost, Jews "from every nation in the whole world" each "heard these men speaking his own native language" (Acts 2:5–11). The Greek word for the crowd's "confusion" (synechythē, Acts 2:6) is from the same verb the Septuagint uses for "mix up" in Genesis 11:7, 9. Many readers since the early church have seen Pentecost as Babel's answer: the nations are not forced back into one language but united in one Spirit while keeping their languages. Zephaniah 3:9 promises that God will give the peoples "a pure speech" to call on the LORD, and Revelation 7:9 pictures every tribe and language before the throne.

a: This is the family history of Shem
p: From Shem to Terah lifespans fall sharply, though not evenly,, from 600 to 205 years.
b: By the Hebrew numbers, lifespans drop sharply, though not evenly, after the flood: Shem 600, Arpachshad 438, Shelah 433, Eber 464, then after Peleg (in whose days "the earth was split up," 10:25) about 239, 239, 230, 148, and Terah 205. Abraham lives 175 years (25:7), Moses 120 (Deuteronomy 34:7). Young-earth writers see this curve as real history after the flood. Others see a literary pattern bringing humans down to the normal limit of 6:3. Like chapter 5, the list has ten generations from Shem to Abram, and the Septuagint and the Samaritan Pentateuch give very different numbers (see the variants at 11:12 and the chapter page).

a: Arpachshad lived 35 years and fathered Shelah
p: Luke's family tree of Jesus has a Cainan between Arpachshad and Shelah, as the Septuagint does.
b: Luke 3:35–36 traces Jesus' line: "...the son of Shelah, the son of Cainan, the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem..." The Masoretic Text, the Samaritan Pentateuch and 1 Chronicles 1:18, 24 have no Cainan here; the Septuagint adds him in Genesis 10:24 and 11:12–13 (see the variants there). Luke used the Greek Bible, so he followed its list. Some scholars think the extra Cainan was a copying error in the Greek, repeating the Cainan (Kenan) of 5:9; others, including some young-earth writers, defend him as original. The question matters for those who build a chronology from these lists: either the Hebrew lost a name, or the Greek and Luke added one.

a: Terah lived 70 years and fathered Abram, Nahor and Haran
p: Abram is listed first, but he may not be the oldest. The numbers raise a puzzle that Acts 7:4 touches.
b: Abram is named first for importance, as Shem is in 5:32. If Terah died at 205 in Haran (11:32), and Abram left Haran at 75 (12:4) after his father's death (Acts 7:4), then Abram was born when Terah was 130, not 70. The Samaritan Pentateuch solves this by giving Terah's age at death as 145 (see the variant at 11:32). Jewish tradition kept the Hebrew numbers and said Abram left while Terah was still alive (Rashi on 11:32), with the story told out of order. Joshua 24:2 says that Terah "served other gods," which the rabbis turned into stories of Abram smashing his father's idols (Genesis Rabbah 38:13).

p: A great Sumerian city in southern Iraq. The name "Chaldeans" belongs to a later age.
b: Ur (Tell el-Muqayyar) was excavated by Leonard Woolley from 1922 to 1934, who found its ziggurat of the moon god Nanna (Sin) and royal tombs from about 2500 BC. The Chaldeans (Akkadian Kaldu) appear in records only from the 800s BC, so "of the Chaldeans" is either a later explanatory note (the view of most traditional scholars) or a sign of a late date (the view of most critical scholars). Some, following an old local tradition and Cyrus Gordon, place Abram's Ur in the north, at Urfa (Şanlıurfa) in Turkey, near Haran. Jewish legend read ur as "fire" and told how Nimrod threw Abram into a furnace and Haran died in it (Rashi; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan; Genesis Rabbah 38:13).

t: The barren mother of the promise
p: Chapter 11 ends on a closed womb. The whole promise to Abram will depend on it opening.
b: The narrator says it twice: she was barren; she had no child. Right after this God promises Abram a great nation (12:2). Barrenness becomes a pattern for the women through whom God's promise comes: Rebekah (25:21), Rachel (29:31), Samson's mother (Judges 13:2), Hannah (1 Samuel 1:2) and Elizabeth (Luke 1:7). Each birth shows that the promised line comes by God's gift. Paul uses Sarah's barrenness to explain faith: Abraham believed God "who gives life to the dead" (Romans 4:17–21; compare Isaiah 54:1; Galatians 4:27).
r: Genesis 12:2; Genesis 18:11–14; Genesis 25:21; Genesis 29:31; 1 Samuel 1:2; Luke 1:7; Romans 4:17–21; Galatians 4:27

a: They came as far as Haran
p: Haran, in southern Turkey, was a center of moon worship, like Ur.
b: Haran (Harran) lay on a trade route in upper Mesopotamia, near the Turkish-Syrian border today. Like Ur, it was a center of the moon god Sin, a link that may explain why the family stopped there. Several family names resemble moon-related words: Terah may echo yareach, "moon," and Sarai and Milcah are like Sharratu and Malkatu, titles of the moon god's consort and daughter. Many scholars accept these links; others think they are too uncertain. The place name Haran (Charan in Hebrew) is spelled differently from the person Haran (Haran). Abraham's family stays there for a generation (24:10; 27:43).

p: Genesis never says why Terah's family left Ur. In Judith, Achior says they left to worship the God of heaven.
b: Genesis says only that Terah's family set out from Ur for Canaan and stopped at Haran. It gives no reason. The book of Judith, which Catholic and Orthodox Christians include in the Old Testament, fills the gap. There Achior, an Ammonite leader, tells the Assyrian general the story of Israel. He says the family "did not want to follow the gods of their ancestors who were in the land of the Chaldeans" (Judith 5:7). They "worshiped the God of heaven," were thrown out, and fled to Mesopotamia, where Haran lay (Judith 5:8). So Judith makes the move from Ur an act of faith. Joshua 24:2 says the family had once served other gods.
